I Found the 11 Best Running Shoes for Women for Every Type of Run

📅 07 Dec 2023 | ⏱️ 19 min read (3756 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Womenshealthmag

⏱️ ~19 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in.
  • LOW-IMPACT EXERCISES might be forever buzzy, but the running community is going stronger than ever.
  • In a recent development, as a former competitive runner who still throws down high mileage (50 to 60 miles weekly), I’ve learned the right footwear is crucial for allowing you to continue to pound the pavement, and selecting the right kind of running shoe is important, too.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

LOW-IMPACT EXERCISES might be forever buzzy, but the running community is going stronger than ever. From 5Ks to marathons, lots of women are lacing up to go for a run and getting all the physical and mental health benefits that come with it. Data suggests running is great for everything from cardiovascular fitness to a healthier mindset, and it may even lower your risk of eight major diseases, making it a solid fitness habit to get into. And then there’s the fact that running makes you feel like you’ve accomplished something amazing (because you have).

In a recent development, as a former competitive runner who still throws down high mileage (50 to 60 miles weekly), I’ve learned the right footwear is crucial for allowing you to continue to pound the pavement, and selecting the right kind of running shoe is important, too. The best running shoes for women provide support and cushioning, with the perfect level of fit to help you forget about your footwear while you run.

Recent findings suggest that while you can skimp on some fitness gear, a quality pair of running shoes is an vital investment, according to Melissa Lockwood, DPM, a podiatrist at Heartland Foot and Ankle Associates in Bloomington, Illinois “I am very much in the camp of paying for a really good pair of running shoes,” she says. “It can help really minimize injury in the future.” (Still, if you’re on a tight budget or just want to save a buck, these are our favorite cheap running shoes.).

But, before taking the plunge on racking up miles, it’s vital to figure out what kind of heel-to-toe drop, toe box, stability, cushioning, and heel stack is best for you. Finding the perfect running shoes involves understanding how specific design elements impact your comfort, performance, and overall experience.

There is no right or wrong, as everyone has different needs (and those needs for running shoes differ from walking shoes), but we'll go over the most vital factors to consider when shopping for running shoes.

Hoka does it right when it comes to a durable, high-quality shoe—specifically the Clifton 11, which was released in July 2026 in tandem with the higher-performance-oriented Clifton Pro. The Clifton family has been a crowd pleaser in the running community and amongst WH editors for a long time, and with good reason.

Recent findings suggest that the Clifton 11 is considered one of the brand’s most versatile running shoes, making it a good fit for everyone from beginners to seasoned pros. WH style editor Shannon Zitz claims her feet never felt fatigued while she was testing this shoe, even with plantar fasciitis. “There’s technically a rocker shape built into the sole, but it's subtle enough that I barely noticed it—instead, my stride just felt smooth and natural whether I was walking or running,” she says.

The Clifton 11 has an eight-millimeter heel-to-toe drop to help alleviate pressure on the plantar fascia, and the brand shaved off almost half an ounce from the weight of the model’s previous version, the Clifton 10, primarily through weight-saving revisions to the shoe’s upper. This was the primary change, with Hoka keeping the midsole that we know and love the same.

These shoes offer maximum cushioning you’ll feel—the same EVA foam found in the Bondi 9 without the extra bulk. Just be aware that these don’t offer any stability innovations for flat feet, which is especially essential if you’re prone to overpronation. As for fit, the toe box does run narrow, but luckily, wide sizing is available.

It has been revealed that read More: Hoka Clifton 11 vs. Hoka Clifton Pro.

Industry observers note that on has built an empire out of its highly cushioned Cloudmonster line. But its most cushioned shoe of all is the Cloudmonster 3 Hyper, an impressively bouncy sneaker that’ll make you feel like a gazelle bounding down the street.

It has been revealed that it’s generally accepted that the more cushioning a shoe has, the heavier its weight (because of all that foam packed into the midsole). But the On Cloudmonster 3 Hyper manages to deliver a highly cushioned shoe in a relatively lightweight 7.5 oz package. The result is a next-level energy return that feels like it’s propelling you forward with each step.

It has been revealed that this sneaker has a soft, breathable upper to minimize foot sweat, along with a highly padded heel collar that lowers the risk of rubbing. I’ve worn a lot of running shoes, and that heel collar may be the thickest I’ve ever seen. There’s a nice, roomy toe box, too.

Recent findings suggest that while there’s a lot to love about the Cloudmonster 3 Hyper, it’s not perfect. This shoe’s $220 price tag puts it out of reach for many, and the tongue is on the thin side (not a deal-breaker, but some people prefer something more padded). Still, if you have the budget for it and like to feel like you’re running on actual clouds, this is a solid choice.

Read More: Best On Walking Shoes.

It has been revealed that think of a daily trainer as the chameleon of the running shoe world. This sneaker needs to be able to be durable enough for regular use, comfortable, and versatile enough to handle higher mileage along with speedier runs. The Adidas Adizero Evo SL was designed with all of that in mind, serving up a highly adaptable shoe that works for nearly everyone. That’s probably why this shoe keeps landing on the feet of runners all over the place.

The Adizero Evo SL has a soft, bouncy feel underfoot and plenty of energy return thanks to Adidas’ proprietary Lightstrike Pro foam packed into the midsole. It’s also relatively lightweight, clocking in at just under 8 oz. The shoe’s peppy sensation and slight rocker shape support your stride but don’t push you forward in a way that feels unnatural.

This sneaker has an engineered mesh upper to let your feet breathe, even when you’re clocking some serious mileage. This shoe has a slightly tapered toe box, which isn’t for everyone. The outsole is also a little flat and isn’t the grippiest you’ll find, but road runners are unlikely to have an glitch. While you’re probably not choosing a running shoe based on looks alone, it doesn’t hurt that the Adizero Evo SL looks sleek.

The best shoe for recovery runs is a total workhorse, delivering enough stability and cushioning to keep you comfortable as you move along at a moderate pace. The Brooks Ghost Max 3 is up for the challenge, with a wide, stable base and supportive feel to take the pressure off your joints.

It has been revealed that this isn’t a stability shoe, per se—it won’t work to correct your stride—but it still creates a sense like you’re not going to roll an ankle or have any other gait issues as you pound the pavement. The Ghost Max 3 is a heavier shoe, although I haven’t noticed any fatigue or extra drag in it. But this sneaker holds up well to high-volume running. I wear this regularly and have never noticed any durability issues.

Sources indicate that the Ghost Max 3 features nitrogen-infused DNA Loft v3 foam for support and cushioning. However, it won’t give you a sinking-in feel and there is limited energy return, which could be a pro or con, depending on what you’re after. This sneaker also has a jacquard mesh upper that feels a little softer than many other running shoes out there. The Ghost Max 3 provides plenty of room, from the midfoot to the toe box, making it a good fit for people with wider feet. Just don’t proposal to do any speed work in this shoe—it’s a little too heavy for that.

Read More: Brooks Ghost Max 3 Review.

It has been revealed that it's clear that Lululemon’s Wildfeel was designed by people who actually do trail running. It has features you want in a trail running shoe beyond just good grip.

There’s a knitted sock-like upper that molds to your foot to keep out pebbles and other debris, along with a toe bumper to protect your feet over rugged terrain. I took these shoes on several runs over a rocky trail near my house, along with a few beach runs, and was impressed at how well it kept the stuff outside from getting into my shoe.

The Wildfeel has a dual-density midsole, which means that it helps give you a feeling of moving forward when you're going up hills and absorbs impact when you’re going down.

Industry observers note that like many other Lululemon shoes, the toe box runs a little narrow. My heel slipped around a little when I first wore these shoes, although that’s pretty common in a trail shoe, and it got better with time and more wear.

Read More: Best Trail Running Shoes.

There’s a wide range of shoes that consider themselves “stability” sneakers, but the Hoka Arahi 8 does a solid job correcting your stride with each step without being annoying. Many stability shoes are clunky and heavy, but the Arahi 8 manages to be lightweight at just 7.7 oz.

The Arahi 8 features a lot of changes from the previous version, the Arahi 7. This shoe uses special H-frame technology, featuring foam at the inner and outer foot, to deliver a more balanced support system. It’s roomy and comfortable, too. But this shoe is clearly not for everyone.

In a recent development, the level of stability is high, and that constant gait correction may feel like too much for some people. It also isn’t very responsive, so you’re not getting much back from your shoe with each stride other than security. (To be fair, though, that’s what people are usually after with a stability shoe.) Still, the Arahi 8 is impressively cushioned and very comfortable, whether you’re working your way through a long training session or just going out on a daily run.

In a recent development, long runs require plenty of cushioning to support you along the way. The Nike Vomero Plus, which won the award for Best Cushioned Running Shoe in the 2026 Women’s Health Fitness Awards, is here to help. This shoe delivers a fun, bouncy feel that helps propel you as you rack up the miles.

It has been revealed that the Vomero Plus has a roomy toe box and overall comfortable feel, serving up a shoe that makes long runs a little more seamless. That bounciness comes courtesy of Nike’s ZoomX foam, which is positioned along the length of the shoe. The engineered upper is crafted from yarn for a soft, breathable sensation.

It has been revealed that the Vomero Plus provides a grippy outsole, making it perfect for the pavement. But if you’re looking for a stability shoe, the Vomero Plus isn’t it. Its high heel stack and bounciness is too much for that. But if you want a highly cushioned feel as you log some serious miles, this is an excellent choice.

The right race day shoe has the tough challenge of being supportive, cushiony, and lightweight, helping you to hit a PR without feeling like your footwear is holding you back. The Upcoming Balance FuelCell SuperComp Elite v5 is designed with longer-distance racers (think: half and marathon runners) in mind, but can still be an excellent choice for 5Ks and 10Ks thanks to its lightweight (6 oz) construction and solid energy return.

Let’s get this out of the way now: At $265, this is not a cheap shoe. With that, it’s unlikely to be a good investment for the occasional racer. But if your weekends are booked with road races, it’s worth at least considering.

This shoe delivers a locked-in feel, along with great traction to give you more confidence, even over wet surfaces. The roomy toe box and breathable upper also reinforce the FuelCell SuperComp Elite v5’s comfortable feel. This shoe is stable without sacrificing punchiness, helping you to feel supported as you stride. Just be aware that the midfoot and heel may feel a little too narrow for those with wider feet. But, luckily, this sneaker is available in wide widths, too.

Read More: Best Running Shoes for Plantar Fasciitis.

Industry observers note that the lululemon Beyondfeel running shoes truly live up to their name. They’re comfortable at the heels (and everywhere), with a heel stack that provides just the right amount of cushioning. It absorbs impact while still feeling responsive, especially during long runs. Plus, the cushioning around the ankle delivers security in every step.

The heel-to-toe drop is also a game changer—it really makes a difference for runners who heel-strike. Instead of feeling the usual jarring sensation from heel-striking, there are smooth transitions from each step. The bounce in the heel also makes it easier to maintain a steady stride without losing momentum, which is a huge benefit for runners who naturally land on their heels. The shoes guide feet to strike with the midfoot instead of the heel.

These shoes feel slightly bouncy while you run, and offer decent grip for trails and roads, making for a versatile running shoe. If you’re an overpronator, this isn’t the shoe for you—it doesn’t provide enough medial support (on the inside of the shoe). But it’s got plenty of features to make running a dream for heel strikers.

Read More: Best lululemon Shoes Ranked.

In a recent development, there’s a range in severity with overpronators, and what works for one won’t work for everyone. But the Asics Gel-Nimbus 28 does a solid job trying to please everyone in the overpronation camp. This shoe delivers a feel that’s not too soft or too firm, giving you the support and stability you need without feeling like you’re in a “special” shoe.

Sources indicate that this shoe is lightweight for a stability shoe at 8.5 oz, making it good for most runs that don’t involve speed work. It also delivers a solid, locked-in sensation to make you feel secure with each step. The shoe’s OrthoLite sockliner also supports that cozier feel. The Gel-Nimbus 28 feels slightly springy underfoot, which is rare for a stability shoe. (Still, the overall effect isn’t very responsive compared to non-stability shoes.).

Recent findings suggest that asics in general tends to run narrow and the Gel-Nimbus 28 is no exception. If your feet tend to teeter between regular and wide sizes, you may want to consider hedging your bets and trying out a larger size.

The best shoe for speed work is very different from what you need for distance training or even race day. The Saucony Endorphin Azura is a lightweight (7.5 oz) shoe with a snappy feel that still manages to make you feel stable and locked in as you zip around.

Sources indicate that the Saucony Endorphin Azura uses Pebax foam to create a responsive, bouncy feel, making you feel a little faster than usual. It also has a wide and stable base for added security during training. While it’s designed for speed, you can still comfortably wear this sneaker for longer runs and daily mileage. Just be aware that the shoe’s special SpeedRoll technology may feel slightly awkward at slower speeds.

The Endorphin Azura’s outsole features XT-900 rubber for a grippy feel underfoot, making you feel comfortable pushing the pace. Saucony shoes are known for a narrower fit, and the Endorphin Azura is no exception. If you have wider feet, it may be best to look elsewhere. (It unfortunately doesn’t come in wide sizes.).

Maximum Cushioning: This type of cushion feels amazingly plush and has excellent shock absorption, which is essential for long-distance running. While they’re designed to minimize the impact on the joints, they’re not the best for speed workouts unless the shoe has a lower heel-to-toe drop and some firmness.

Sources indicate that medium: If you want to balance speed with stability, medium cushioning is ideal. Too much cushioning can cause runners with flat feet to overpronate more from the bulkiness and softness. So, this type of cushioning is best if you want a more aligned gait.

Sources indicate that this is the difference in height between the heel and front part (known as the forefoot) of the shoe. It can impact how your foot lands on the ground when you run. Low drops (0 to 4 mm) are flatter and encourage a natural running style where you land in the middle or front of your foot. They’re great if you like to feel close to the ground, enjoy trail running, or prefer a minimalist shoe design. Medium drop (5 to 8 mm) is a versatile option that offers mid-height and cushioning—this works well for most running styles. High drop (9 to 12 mm) tends to have more height in the heel to absorb impact (this is great for heel-strikers).

This is the height of the cushion under the heel. It’s measured from the outsole (the bottom of the shoe) to the insole (where your foot rests). Higher stacks offer more softness for long-distance running or for those who need less impact on the joints. Prioritizing this means sacrificing ground feel, and for some, that may feel unbalanced given the additional height.

Sources indicate that running shoes can provide a slew of benefits to suit your feet, but podiatrists stress the importance of getting a well-fitting shoe. “The shoe should fit your foot well and not cause any rubbing on the toes,” notes Richard H. Graves, DPM, a podiatrist at Sol Foot & Ankle Centers in Long Beach, California “They should feel comfortable immediately upon putting them on and walking around.”.

Consider these areas of the shoe when checking the fit:.

Toe Box: This is the front part of the shoe where the toes sit. Toes spread naturally when you have extra room in the toe box, and this is especially important during long runs since feet can swell. But if the toe box is too big, it can lead to sliding and instability in the shoes.

Industry observers note that length: Since feet often swell from pounding pavement, it’s a good idea to have about a thumb’s width away from the tip of the shoe to your toe. If you’re unsure of your size, the best bet is to visit a running store to get properly fitted.

Arch Support: Those with flat feet and overpronators (when your foot lands on your outside heel and rolls inward) will want to look for shoes with enough firmness and high arch support to help keep feet aligned. Too much cushioning can create an unbalanced feeling, which can further aggravate pain. Those with neutral to high arches will have no problems wearing shoes with neutral support. Most shoes specify which arch type they accommodate, so make sure to read their product descriptions. And, definitely don’t wear shoes with no arch support—your feet need support.

Industry observers note that the type of running workouts you initiative to do will dictate elements like cushioning, support, and weight. More cushioning is often better with daily training and distance runs. You may also get away with a slightly heavier (but not too heavy) shoe, which usually means there’s more cushioning and stability. But shoes for speed work and race day tend to have less cushioning and a lighter weight, making it easier to move faster. For a deep-dive into the topic of running shoe selection, check out our story about how to figure out which type of running shoe you need.

Recent findings suggest that A stability shoe can help correct gait issues like overpronation, which is when your foot rolls inward excessively when you run or walk. Not everyone needs a stability shoe, but some level of stability is key for reducing injury risk when you’re an overpronator. There are a few ways to tell if you overpronate, per Graves: Your feet appear to be rolling inward when you stand in a relaxed position and the heels of shoes you’ve worn are tilted inward.

According to recent reports, you should switch out your running shoes every 300 to 500 miles. An easy way to maximize your shoe lifespan is to have a few pairs that you rotate between runs. Also, if you visually see them degrading, it's time to snag a latest pair.

Running shoes can be washed in cold water in the washing machine with light detergent, or spot-cleaned with a sponge. But, you should never put your shoes in the dryer—they can shrink! Instead, let them air dry in the sun.

In a recent development, A simple at-home way to determine your arch type is the wet footprint test. You simply dip your foot in the water and step onto paper. If you see your entire foot, you have flat feet. Your foot will look like a comma if you have high arches, while a neutral arch will show slight elevation.

I’ve tested dozens of pairs of running shoes to determine which make the cut for the best running shoes for women. As a personal trainer, fitness writer, and runner with years of experience testing running shoes, I put each pair to the test during two-mile runs where I evaluated key performance factors such as cushioning, stability, comfort, support, traction, and responsiveness. I also considered how well the shoes supported my stride and whether or not they helped me maintain a consistent pace. Additionally, WH fitness editors provided feedback on select shoes they love to wear during training and racing.

#64293. 10 Best Coffee Table Books to Buy in 2026, According to AD

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 13m • 📚 Deep Dive (2685 w)

10 Best Coffee Table Books to Buy in 2026, According to AD

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2685 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Architecturaldigest

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that whether placed on a shelf or the coffee table in your living room, coffee table books can easily serve as pieces of decor.
  • We’ve picked the best coffee table books from this year’s batch, and we’re thrilled to hole up with them until warmer days make their appearance.
  • Sources indicate that there are over 400 pages of inspiration-packed interiors to peruse in Amy Astley’s second coffee table book, AD at Home.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that whether placed on a shelf or the coffee table in your living room, coffee table books can easily serve as pieces of decor. “I feel that books complete any room,” claims global editorial director Amy Astley. “They are a record of your life and passions—I am profoundly connected to all of my printed matter!”.

We’ve picked the best coffee table books from this year’s batch, and we’re thrilled to hole up with them until warmer days make their appearance. Here are our favorites from 2026’s bountiful assortment of debuts—many of them featuring AD-approved talents—all packed with invaluable design insights and gorgeous interiors past and present.

Sources indicate that there are over 400 pages of inspiration-packed interiors to peruse in Amy Astley’s second coffee table book, AD at Home. Throughout the book you’ll find dreamy pictures and thoughtful essays pulled straight from our pages, including anecdotes from former cover stars like Marc Jacobs, Dakota Johnson, Gwyneth Paltrow, and more. “Even in a world of oversharing on social media, there is still such a frisson of entree in glimpsing the private world of a public figure, and AD will eternally share the fantasy,” Astley states in her editor’s letter. With the holidays approaching, we think AD at Home also makes a perfect gift for the collector, the design enthusiast, and anyone who’s just a little bit nosy about what’s going on behind a celebrity’s closed doors.

Recent findings suggest that created by AD France’s former editor-in-chief, Marie Kalt, La Bibliothèque de l’Amateur is a collection of compact, accessible monographs devoted to the great names of 20th-century design. The contents explore the work of acclaimed designers, including Alvar Aalto, Charlotte Perriand, Ettore Sottsass, while including emerging talents in the conversation as well. Each $30 volume pairs a brief introduction with about 60 images and detailed captions, offering an engaging visual primer on a designer’s life and work.

Global features director Sam Cochran’s debut coffee table book opens with the words, “Nothing is interesting unless it is personal.” His project, American Designers at Home, brings that idea to life beautifully. The volume takes you inside the homes of 20 leading designers across the country—including Andre Mellone, Kelly Wearstler, and Robin Standefer and Stephen Alesch of Roman and Williams—each reflecting its creator’s distinctive taste and personal passions. “As my dear friend Markham Roberts—one of the designers featured in the book—says, ‘If stuff makes you happy, you want it around,’ and this book makes me very happy,” says global interiors and garden director Alison Levasseur.

Levasseur says that Simon Upton’s most recent release with Rizzoli contains “beauty and poetry on every page.” The title is a nod to the iconic London A–Z: The detailed street atlas that every Londoner seemed to own in the 1980s and early 2000s, pre-Google Maps. Like its namesake, Upton’s book is an expert guide, specifically to a world of extraordinary interiors and visual pleasures. “Some of my favorite stories ever to appear in the pages of AD were photographed by Upton,” says Levasseur. “Many are gathered here, including those featuring Adwoa Aboah, Dakota Johnson, and Sienna Miller.”.

According to recent reports, this beautiful debut monograph not only showcases Chicago architect Joan Craig's elegant classical architecture, but it also spotlights the artistry behind it. “I love that Craig shares the spotlight with the often-unsung craftspeople who bring her interiors to life, including Brittany’s masters of straw marquetry and Bologna’s terrazzo artisans,” says senior digital editor Catherine Hong. “It's a tribute to design excellence and also the art of collaboration.".

“Whether or not you’d ever dare to decorate with Sasha Bikoff’s over-the-top flair, this book is guaranteed to make a splash on your coffee table,” says Hong. Behind its trippy, hot-pink cover lies screaming color, clashing eras, and utter fantasy. The designer lives by her “Rule of Three Wows”—chronicled in the pages—and her book is, accordingly, loud, wildly fun, and a little bit insane in the best way.

Studio Valle de Valle’s debut monograph offers a refined window into the AD100 firm’s singular vision and creative evolution—surveying 10 projects from the past 10 years. Printed in Italy, with photography by Stephen Kent Johnson, the pages demonstrate the firm’s interior philosophy of creating spaces that feel personal, layered, and deeply inhabitable. “The edition isn’t just a tour de visual force, it’s an art object unto itself,” says Cochran. “I would expect nothing less from these brilliant auteurs.".

“One of Meyer Davis’s greatest strengths is how cofounders Will Meyer and Gray Davis distill references, ideas, and desires into a highly refined vision,” says AD PRO senior editor Mel Studach. As client Jenna Lyons puts it in the book’s foreword, “They gave me clarity.” Beyond a printed body of work, The Language of Home is a testament to the collaborations that shape the studio's warm, reductive interiors. Designed with honest materials and a contemporary lens, the featured residences—a modern glass house in the Berkshires and an earthen dwelling in Puerto Escondido—reflect their inhabitants with a calm, clear ease.

The inaugural monograph from AD100 design duo Humbert & Poyet showcases their signature brand of eclectic French luxury, blending Art Deco glamour, midcentury modernism, and the decorative arts. Spanning residential and hospitality projects around the world, the book takes readers from a French Riviera villa to a Milan restaurant housed in a 17th-century chapel, with stops in New York, Paris, Monaco, and Seoul.

In Newly introduced York: Atelier AM, Alexandra and Michael Misczynkski, the married couple behind the AD100 firm, shine a light on their New York projects, all beautifully captured by François Halard. Spotlighting a range of projects like elegant Manhattan residences and more relaxed Long Island retreats, contributor Ingrid Abramovitch says the book itself is “equally exquisite, with a cover resembling wood grain, and high-gloss pages printed in Italy.”.

Industry observers note that 2026 AD Newly introduced American Voices honoree Amber Guyton first burst onto the design scene by way of her hit blog, Blessed Little Bungalow. “Her debut book brings the same wit and spirit to the printed page in a kaleidoscope of color and pattern,” states Cochran. Senior shopping editor Nashia Baker adds that the pages “truly embody how to bring personality to any room.” Throughout the book, she makes a case for maximalism, and distills her approach into four pillars: joy, culture, layers, and intention.

Industry observers note that “This book is perfect for cinephiles, design-lovers, or anyone with a case of wanderlust,” says senior digital editor Rachel Wallace. Film is one way to travel the world without ever leaving the sofa, and with her new project On Location, longtime AD contributor Cathy Whitlock takes readers on a global cinematic journey. The book goes behind the scenes of films that make you want to hop on a flight and never look back. Colorful Mexico City scenes from Frida and Marie Antoinette’s famous Palace of Versailles shooting location are both represented.

One of the few completely fail-proof gifts is one of the best coffee table books of the season—weighty tomes whose thick, glossy pages feature stunning photographs and illustrations, to be specific. On a superficial level, they add ambiance, whether you place them in a library or a living room. But the best ones live in your home forever, while expanding your horizons far beyond. They also come across as far more memorable and thoughtful than the expected candle or bottle of champagne. Like works of fiction, there are limitless topics that can make deciding on an eye-catching hardcover (that doubles as home decor) seemingly impossible.

But that’s where we come in. Our team has gathered its favorite giftable recommendations for everyone from tennis enthusiasts to globe-trotters to interior design aficionados. From a book focused on hotels around the world to another that spotlights Tokyo style, there are plenty of ways to adorn the coffee tables of all the people on your holiday gift list. Most of them came out in 2024, but we’ve also included a few evergreen picks that make worthy gifts any year.

Plus, if you’re down to the wire on last-minute gifts, rest assured that most of these selections are available (and even marked down ahead of the holidays!) on Amazon.

Après-ski style needs no introduction in a season full of fuzzy Fair Isle sweaters, but it’s the cozy interiors of the chalets along the world’s most popular ski slopes that are worthy of a second look. From the wooden beams of an A-frame to the blazing fireplaces set within them, AD contributor Kathryn O’Shea-Evans pores over the finer details in this fun, wintery escape.

As associate digital editor Maya Ibbitson previously described it, “Alpine Style is a true compendium of resort luxury,” spanning spectacular chalets from Gstaad to Aspen and featuring the works of AD PRO Directory members such as Massucco Warner, Robbins Architecture, and Kara Adam Interiors.

Japan’s interiors are a perpetual reference for modern-day designers, and whether you’re a proponent of wabi-sabi principles or just looking for small space ideas, Tokyo Style will help you explore both.

Originally published in 1993, it’s since become a collector’s item and cult classic, and it was recommended by commerce writer Julia Harrison for anyone who would appreciate a more intimate glimpse of Tokyo’s dwellings: “Apartamento, an imprint that consistently delivers on elite design, has reintroduced Tsuzuki’s collection for us to enjoy in its full brilliance—that is, not a ‘fine’ condition original at $170 with $90 shipping from eBay.”.

Prefaced with a foreword by Spike Lee, BLK MKT Vintage peers into the world of the Brooklyn antique shop’s endlessly curious founders Jannah Handy and Kiyanna Stewart. “This monograph teems with more than 300 studies of vintage ephemera and reads like a collage with context, or an I spy for your inner adult archivist,” writes Ibbitson of the book. For collectors, Sydney Gore pinpoints it as a must-have for your rotation.

Donald Judd’s considered, minimalist approach to design has fostered its own cult of acolytes who, these days, emulate his daybeds and chairs on Instagram.

Sources indicate that for the true Juddheads, the Judd Foundation has produced a fresh book edited by his children Rainer and Flavin Judd that chronicles more than one hundred of his functional works produced between 1970 and 1992. “Mixed in are the juiciest bits: photos from past and present of those pieces in Judd-designed spaces in New York and Marfa,” Ibbitson writes.

AD’s Milan correspondent Laura May Todd penned a delightful homage to Italian living this year, one which spans from historic palaces in Venice to the homes of creatives like Luca Guadagnino along with midcentury Milanese apartments, so you can enjoy a small taste of la dolce vita on each page.

It was one of the AD PRO team’s favorite book releases this fall, one which should suit the person on your list who never got over their Italian study abroad or is manifesting a Sicilian villa in their future.

For the person on your list who delights in having people over, How They Entertain, released this fall, serves as a comprehensive guide to (and celebration of) the art of hosting.

Written by Pierre Sauvage, it’s chock-full of inspiration for your next dinner party, from recipes to design notes on arranging a tabletop to remember, as well as interviews with tastemakers like Laura Gonzalez about their particular philosophy on entertaining guests.

Considering this year’s smash summer hit Challengers and the enduring popularity of tenniscore (polos, skorts, and all), it’s clear that tennis is a lifestyle that has captured the imagination of many people, avid tennis players or not.

This book recommended by the AD PRO team earlier this year is dedicated to a more, uh, underserved cross section of the sport: the backdrops where athletes volley their way to tournament glory (clay, grass, asphalt, and beyond) in locales from Queens to Kenya.

AD100 designer Jeremiah Brent is no stranger to the pages of this very magazine, and his latest book is a friends and family affair studded with stars, like Oprah and legendary choreographer Fatima Robinson, with whom Brent has formed close connections over the past 20 years.

We’ve previously described the book (layered with sentimental photos and newly introduced snapshots of contributors in their home) as “more scrapbook than design manifesto, a love letter to the spaces that people have inhabited and inherited over the years.” Read AD’s extensive interview with Brent for more backstory behind (and tidbits from) the book.

It has been revealed that for art buffs with a fondness for the Harlem Renaissance—an era synonymous with greats like Aaron Douglas, known as the father of African-American art—this fresh book compiled by MoMA curator Denise Murrell is an excellent title to know. “Having this book is about as close as you’ll ever get to owning one of the original masterpieces featured in the Harlem Renaissance exhibition at The Met,” Gore indicates.

Self-interested plug here, but we really couldn’t publish a guide to coffee table books without mentioning our own, AD at 100: A Century of Style. For the design buff with an appetite for lush interiors and a healthy curiosity for how A-listers live, there’s no more satisfying holiday treat than this tome that delves into the homes of the Obamas, David Hockney, Diana Vreeland, and beyond. It also serves as a bird’s eye view of a century in design and architecture, including the works of Frank Gehry, David Hicks, Frank Lloyd Wright, and much, much more.

Architecture has a reputation for myopia when it comes to its foremost voices, but this book seeks to rectify the past with a fresh overview of some of its most brilliant underrepresented talents, including interviews with female architects around the globe such as Tatiana Bilbao, Liz Diller, and Julia Gamolina.

“100 Women offers a refreshing reframe of the built environment outside of the male-dominated Western canon, proving the benefits of sourcing alternative points of reference,” Ibbitson wrote of it in AD PRO’s guide to the best upcoming design books out this past spring.

It has been revealed that colony founder Jean Lin has mentored and platformed some of the design world’s brightest rising stars, and in her first book out this year, she tapped a wide pool of creatives to explore the concept of collections that inform their work, from ceramicist Stephanie H. Shih’s cache of soy sauce bottles to Mira Nakashima’s stockpile of lumber inherited from her father, architect turned furniture maker George Nakashima.

Sources indicate that that’s just one facet of the book Ibbitson previously described as an “encyclopedic, elemental study of artist studios, profiles, materials, and everything else under the design umbrella,” with plenty of wisdom imparted within its pages, from how-tos to styling tips. Read our interview with Lin for more of her notes on curating a collection of your own.

Luna Luna—a 1980s artist-led amusement park featuring works by icons of the art world such as Jean-Michel Basquiat, Keith Haring, Salvador Dalí, and David Hockney—is experiencing a resurgence as of late, what with a newly introduced retrospective at The Shed this year, along with a revival of the park itself in Los Angeles late last year.

In a recent development, this 2023 book takes a deeper dive into Luna Luna’s history blending fine art with the playful energy of a carnival—encompassing rides, interactive installations, and surreal sculptures. It comes recommended by associate visuals editor Shani Kravetz, who nods to the book’s breadth of archival media within, from photos to sketches, that are accompanied by behind-the-scenes stories.

According to recent reports, for jet-setters who love to live large on vacation, Spencer Bailey’s Design: The Leading Hotels of the World (released just this month) is one sure way to sustain a sense of wanderlust. His fresh book takes readers on a visual journey to 80 countries around the globe, inviting them to mentally book into sumptuous spaces from The Okura in Tokyo to the Portrait Hotel in Milan. It’s rounded out by notable travel and design writers like Maria Cristina Didero and Mark Ellwood, who lend us their travel tips, on top of their reflections on the lodgings featured within.

The 10 Best Skincare Brands for Men in 2026, According to a Grooming Editor

📅 12 Dec 2023 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3118 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Menshealth

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that AS A GROOMING editor, I’m constantly testing products from both emerging brands and classic favorites, which culminates in two major outcomes.
  • Sources indicate that in recent years, the men’s grooming industry has been exploding, with upcoming options dropping every week.
  • It has been revealed that the good news is that there are now plenty of options out there for every guy, but cutting through the noise to find what actually works can be a hassle.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that AS A GROOMING editor, I’m constantly testing products from both emerging brands and classic favorites, which culminates in two major outcomes. First, I’m regularly discovering new and exciting ingredients that I’m allergic to (please patch test—do as I say, not as I do, etc.). But more importantly, I’ve come to be intimately familiar with which brands are consistently putting out the best-feeling and overall most effective products to include in your daily skincare routine.

Sources indicate that in recent years, the men’s grooming industry has been exploding, with upcoming options dropping every week. As a result, there have never been more brands available, and choosing which to try has never been more overwhelming. The shelves are packed with a selection of skincare products which, let’s get real, can feel a little daunting.

It has been revealed that the good news is that there are now plenty of options out there for every guy, but cutting through the noise to find what actually works can be a hassle. To ease this decision-making tension when choosing serums, moisturizers, soaps, or other grooming products, these are the best brands for men.

Industry observers note that I love Marlowe products mainly because the brand never overthinks this whole skincare thing. Its products are simple and effective. The creams are smooth and long-lasting without being heavy; the soaps are deeply cleansing with strong lathers, and the deodorants smell great while providing day-long protection.

It has been revealed that the brand heavily features natural ingredients (which I love) and never includes any irritating chemicals like parabens or phthalates (which my sensitive skin hates). Not to mention, many of the products are sustainably packaged, including the soap wrappers, which are made of 100 percent recycled materials. Simply put, when I’m browsing the skincare aisle (or more accurately, Amazon’s skincare page), Marlowe is the most reliable brand I can find time after time.

Product Highlight: The Marlowe No. 102 Body Scrub Soaps get a lot of love thanks to their clean formulas backed by always-moisturizing green tea, shea butter, and olive oil, as well as incredible, cologne-quality scents like santal or oud wood. Not to mention, insanely strong lathers that help these bars last for weeks.

Sources indicate that but if I had to pick one facial moisturizer to wear for the rest of my life, it’d probably be the No. 128 Daily Face Lotion with SPF 50. Not only is it the best SPF moisturizer around, but it’s also one of the most nourishing, hydrating, and non-irritating moisturizers, full stop, SPF or not.

Sources indicate that read More: Marlowe No. 128 Daily Face Lotion Review.

Sources indicate that founded in 1965, Baxter of California is one of the oldest grooming brands on this list. As a result, it has a wide range of skincare solutions, but has really been able to zero in on options for sensitive skin over the years.

The brand’s most notable skincare products are all either fragrance-free, like theOil-Free Moisturizerand Daily Face Wash, or mildly scented so as not to irritate skin, like the Exfoliating Body Wash. And while the latter’s oak moss and cedar scent is certainly subtle, it’s also delightfully woodsy and lasts much longer than its initial intensity would suggest.

Product Highlight: The facial scrub is backed by walnut shell powder, which helps shrink pores and absorb oil, and moisturizing avocado oil to create a gentle, soothing exfoliation. The container is also barely over $20 and lasts forever, as you only need a small dime-sized dose to cover your entire face.

According to recent reports, if your skin is prone to dryness, there’s a good chance that you already have some La Roche-Posay in your medicine cabinet. But if you haven’t tried the brand and you often battle flakes, redness, or other complications associated with dry skin, I can say with no hyperbole that I’m about to change your life. La Roche-Posay products heavily feature skin-soothing gems like niacinamide, glycerin, and ceramides, all of which help restore the skin's moisture barrier and promote a healthy microbiome.

It has been revealed that the creams feel as gentle as any I’ve tested, and most are fragrance-free to avoid any unnecessary irritation. Not to mention, the brand has more products officially accepted by the National Eczema Association than I can count (I also hate doing math, but that’s beside the point). You simply won’t find better skincare for dry skin than La Roche-Posay.

Industry observers note that product Highlight: Speaking of the brand’s plethora of National Eczema Association-approved products, the Lipikar AP+M Triple Repair Body Moisturizer is specifically designed to combat dry skin with a formula featuring soothing shea butter and glycerin, ceramide-3 to strengthen and protect the skin’s natural barrier, and niacinamide with its anti-inflammatory properties.I’m prone to dry skin pretty much everywhere (especially during the cooler months), but I lather this stuff on twice a day, and it’s barely an concern anymore. Plus, it absorbs faster than any other body lotion I’ve tried.

Read More: La Roche-Posay Anthelios UVDefense Sunscreen SPF 50 with BEMT Review.

This UK-based skincare brand is heavy on the science and uses its own labs to develop products focused on keeping your skin healthy in the most effective way possible. Built on three pillars—sun protection, vitamin C, and retinol—these products not only help your skin live its best life now, but protect it from signs of aging in the future.

It’s an extensive line with popular favorites like the Crystal Retinal Ceramide Eye Cream, C-Tetra Vitamin C Serum, and the Advanced Night Ceramide Cream to set your skin up for success.

Product Highlight: Of all the best-sellers mentioned, there is none I ride harder for than the Crystal Retinal Ceramide Eye. You may have noticed the retinal in that title, rather than the far more common retinol, but that isn’t a typo. Just like retinol, retinal is a vitamin A derivative with anti-aging and acne-fighting properties. It’s a slightly more potent vitamin A derivative, however, meaning two things.

It has been revealed that one, it’ll clear skin and reward it with additional elasticity even more successfully than retinol options. And two, it’s way easier (and more harmful) to overuse than retinol, so take it slow and easy if you’re new to the ingredient. Too much product can result in irritation and drying (been there!), which is not fun.

In a recent development, you’ll likely find this French grooming brand in the medicine cabinet of your coolest, most in-the-know friend. It’s a Parisian-born brand that merges the French sensibility of simplicity with modern natural ingredients.

What started with highly effective and pleasant-to-use face products (try the Mattifying Face Moisturizer and Anti-Dark Circle Cleanser) has now expanded to beard products like luxuriously scented beard oils, body lotion, and hair products (even solid shampoo).

Industry observers note that but what we really dig about Horace is the brand’s commitment to offering options for various skin types or unique concerns. In fact, Horace’s website even includes a consultation quiz you can take to ensure you’re set up with a curated list of items to address your specific needs.

Product Highlight: As someone who has struggled with easily irritated skin and redness, I ride hard for Horace’s Balanced Skin Set. It features the Purifying Face Cleanser, which delicately cleanses skin while eliminating excess oil, and the Hyaluronic Acid and Panthenol Serum to then provide immediate moisture, leaving skin feeling softer for longer.

It has been revealed that the trio is then topped off with the Mattifying Face Moisturizer to hydrate and protect skin. Not to mention, it doesn’t leave any greasy residue behind. This routine has eliminated facial redness time after time for me.

Horace also has some great, surprisingly affordable colognes, the highlight of which is Horace Vintage Vanilla. It’s leathery and cozy, perfect for cooler weather.

It has been revealed that what started with a razor designed to minimize ingrown hairs has since exploded into a full-on grooming empire with thoughtful, solution-oriented products to be used from head to toe. The brand was conceived to provide grooming products to men of color, specifically, but these innovative and effective products can be used by all people regardless of skin color or type, like the soothing aloe vera and coconut water infused face and beard wash, or body wash, which is the body wash which we found to be the most moisturizing option available. Best of all, rarely are these products above $15.

Product Highlight: Obviously, Bevel has come a long way from its ingrown hair-fighting origins, but the brand’s exfoliating toner pads are still hard to beat. Thanks to a powerful combination of green tea and 10 percent glycolic acid, they prepare skin for additional products by deeply cleansing and clearing any lingering gunk on the face, while minimizing the risk of ingrown hairs or other blemishes by exfoliating the skin.

Developed by the former president of Kiehl’s, Chris Salgardo, this men’s grooming brand provides innovative and intuitive products that are deceptively simple. The founder developed all the formulas from scratch using natural, non-toxic ingredients, and used his learnings from his years in skincare to create products that don’t just work, but that you actually want to use.

Similar to Horace, Atwater breaks out products by unique needs. However, it’s a bit more streamlined with three simple options: normal/combination, dry, and oily. While the dry and normal options are also stellar, no other brand nails the demands of oily skin better.

Industry observers note that product Highlight: This is led by the Oil Regulator Facial Cleansing Bar and Oil Regulator Facial Moisturizer. The moisturizer is great, as its gel-consistency is both lightweight and non-greasy, so oily folks can use it without fear of residue; however, the cleansing bar is what’s truly special. Most people with oily skin understand the importance of using lightweight, non-greasy moisturizers and creams, but few pinpoint the importance of soap in this journey.

So many standard soaps and washes strip away skin’s natural oils, causing it to overcompensate and produce more sebum (aka how our skin naturally fights dryness) to restore its moisture balance. Not this bar, though—with hero ingredients like charcoal to target excess oil and sebum, and glycerin to restore the skin’s naturally balanced moisture levels, there are few better options for oily skin.

Bravo Sierra started in 2018 with a simple goal: Create military-grade personal care products that can withstand the most extreme conditions without the use of any harsh ingredients like parabens, sulfates, or silicones.

In just a few years, the high-performance brand was offering upgrades on daily essentials like bar soap, body wash, and deodorant with better ingredients, as well as incredible, elevated scents like orris and santal, and bergamot and musk. Bravo Sierra never forgets its military-inspired roots either, donating over $500,000 to veterans organizations since its inception, according to cofounder Benjamin Bernet.

According to recent reports, product Highlight: I’ve written quite a bit about Bravo Sierra’s incredible deodorant and how its unscented option is the best fragrance-free deodorant on the market, but the scented versions are equally great. Whenever I’m going camping or planning a long hike, I turn to Bravo Sierra’s deodorants because they go on clear, contain probiotics to help control bacteria, and truly withstand the elements.

Recent findings suggest that I once competed in a 10k trail run in the rain wearing the bergamot and musk, and you better believe I was the best-smelling dude there post-run, as the scent was still lingering after all that. The brand’s cleansing bar soaps also deserve a shout-out as one of the most multipurpose soaps (formulated for face, hair, and body) while packing the same stellar scent.

It has been revealed that status skincare is a thing, and Aesop pretty much invented it. Using natural ingredients and elevated scents, these products don’t just look good on your bathroom counter; they actually work to cleanse, hydrate, and fortify your skin, hair, and body.

In a recent development, but anyone who has ever used Aesop products knows that, among the slick designs and soothing formulas, the aspect that really stands out is the scents. From the earthy sandalwood blend of the Moroccan Neroli Post-Shave Lotion to the fresh, citrus-scented Bitter Orange Astringent Toner, it’s no wonder the brand sells its own parfum bottles.

Product Highlight: This product selection is wide, so I’d recommend starting with a bundle that features curated product groupings based on skin type and need. But a special shout-out to the Parsley Seed AntiOxidant Intense Serum, which is a perfect do-it-all serum for daily use, and the Coriander Seed Body Cleanser, one of the best-smelling body washes around.

According to recent reports, you probably already know about Harry’s thanks to their hard-to-beat razors and shaving products that revolutionized the cartridge razor game, but if you haven’t explored the brand’s skin, body, and other beard products, you’re missing out. The brand known for inexpensive and easy-to-use shaving solutions now offers an entire range to keep you groomed and fresh from head to toe, including the 2025 Men’s Health Grooming Award-winning black lip balm backed by meadowfoam for lasting moisturization.

Industry observers note that product Highlight: The Exfoliating Face Wash and moisturizing Daily Face Lotion for your mug are a couple of my favorite budget options available. The face wash is especially useful, as it helps minimize any irritation or ingrowns after shaving with the help of hero ingredient, volcanic rock, which works to remove dead skin cells and promote cell turnover.

Recent findings suggest that being a great skincare brand doesn’t necessarily mean all-encompassing. Not every label offers every product, and this is a good thing. I love a wide selection, but nobody can nail everything, even the greats (further reading: Michael Jordan’s baseball career).

Instead, look for brands that have perfected their corner of the skincare world with key products that are specialized to certain objectives, like Bevel with reducing shave irritation or La Roche-Posay with sensitive-skin-friendly creams. This will result in the highest quality options for every skincare need.

According to recent reports, let’s be honest, for many dudes, this is really the main concern when it comes to buying skincare products. Prices can vary substantially across categories, with one moisturizer costing $20, like Marlowe’s No. 128, and another surpassing $50, like Medik8’s C-Tetra Day Cream. Does this mean Medik8 is $30 better and more effective? Not necessarily, but the pricier you go, typically the more specialized the formulas are. So it really comes down to personal preference, need, and budget.

These are generally the basics. That’s not to say they’re lower-quality, just simpler formulas with more wide-ranging attributes. For example, Marlowe’s No. 121 Facial Cleanser is $14 and is uber effective for all skin types. However, if your skin tends to be especially oily and you want a cleanser with a cologne-quality scent, look to Aesop’s Amazing Face Cleanser for $36, which would find itself in the next cost bracket. Speaking of….

In a recent development, in this range, you’ll find plenty of specialized formulas and quality scents. To combat fine lines and wrinkles, especially if you also have sensitive or dry skin, the La Roche-Posay Hyalu B5 Hyaluronic Acid Serum is ideal. However, to provide that level of additional elasticity to your skin without aggravating it, you have to spend a bit more, which is why it’s $40.

The same goes for Atwater’s Eye Armor anti-aging eye cream. This $32 tube offers nourishment and hydration to fight puffiness and wrinkles at a level lower-priced eye creams might struggle with.

According to recent reports, still, the products you’ll find in this range aren’t the most expensive available. Instead, they’re more mid-tier when it comes to cost. Think of them like a frisky four- or five-seed team that can absolutely make a run in the NCAA tournament, rather than the favorite ones or twos—those would be your luxury options.

According to recent reports, now we’re in the high-end zone. If you’re looking at one skincare product that’s over $50, it’ll either be in a humongous Costco-type container or offering a level of luxury other products simply cannot.

There is no shame in surpassing these options if you’re on a budget or have fairly uncomplicated skin with minimal long-term concerns. Just as there is also nothing wrong with indulging for those who are able. You won’t find many night creams more skin-firming or youth-boosting than the Medik8 Advanced Night Ceramide, which is why it’s $78.

Recent findings suggest that as a grooming editor, I’m constantly putting skincare products to the test and evaluating their feel and efficiency. It is quite literally my job. In fact, I drop a recurring column on the latest and greatest fresh products in the field, so it’s safe to say that I’m up to date on brands and their skincare offerings.

For this story specifically, I consulted with my fellow Men’s Health editors, including Style and Reviews Director Christian Gollayan and Style and Reviews Editor Joseph Cheatham, on their overall favorite products and which brands they tend to prioritize when searching for skincare. I also considered top-rated options on e-commerce sites we trust, and cataloged the brands that have consistently ranked high in our other various skincare product roundups.

In all, I’ve personally tested moisturizers, serums, night creams, eye creams, soaps, body washes, and other skincare essentials from over 50 brands to determine which regularly put out the products with the cleanest, most beneficial ingredients, non-irritating formulas, smoothest, best-feeling applications, and long-term effectiveness. Armed with this extensive testing, research, and expertise, I honed in on the following ten brands as the best skincare product producers on the market today.

The Simple Guide to Finding a Weighted Vest You’ll Actually Use

⏱️ ~18 mins left to finish
