📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

Slip on a weighted vest, and suddenly your regular walk, chores, or bodyweight exercises feel a little more rewarding—the extra weight offering a simple boost in effort and making us more aware of the way our bodies maintain balance and stability.

I’m a certified personal trainer, and I sometimes recommend weighted vests to older adult clients as a way to add extra challenge to walking, cardio, and bodyweight exercises. While recent research suggests that weighted vests may not have a dramatic impact on bone density, they’re still a safe and convenient way to increase the load on your muscles and joints, helping you push yourself a little harder than usual.

In a recent development, weighted vests let you add extra resistance to walking, stair climbing, jumping, push-ups, and pull-ups without needing to grip dumbbells or barbells. Some clients even wear them during everyday activities like cleaning, yard work, or mowing the lawn—making fitness a little more functional and, yes, a bit more fun.

That remarked, if you’ve been diagnosed with osteoporosis, consult your doctor before adding a weighted vest to your exercise routine, while folks who are pregnant or experience back, neck, or joint pain should also avoid them.

Sources indicate that before you take the plunge on purchasing a weighted vest, you should consider the resistance level, workouts such as walking or HIIT, and whether materials are sweat-resistant to determine which one is best for you. Ready to get vested?

After testing a handful of weighted vests for weeks, the trophy goes to the Omorpho G-Vest for its remarkable comfort, ideal weight, and sleek design. I spent a week wearing it for my regular lifting sessions and hour-long walks. It’s easy to wear for my normal gym routine, which includes moves such as walking lunges, Copenhagen planks, pull-ups, and push-ups.

However, I found it to be challenging when worn for heavier compound lifts like front squats, deadlifts, and barbell rows. Other than walking lunges, I wouldn’t normally add load to those exercises because of the logistics of holding or hanging weight, but the vest makes it possible to add resistance without gripping anything.

It has been revealed that the fit is another reason the G-Vest earns the top spot. This vest is surprisingly comfortable considering it weighs just over five pounds from stainless steel balls. While the back panels have more weight—226 stainless steel balls on the back and 122 on the front—the weight distribution feels uniform when wearing.

It’s also compact—from the shoulder straps to the bottom of the vest is about 17 inches, which, for me, is great since I have a very short torso. It also doesn't dig into the top of my hip bone when I move around.

Even if you don’t have a short torso, you’ll still appreciate the soft-to-the-touch polyester fabric, despite it feeling like neoprene (synthetic rubber). I use adjustable cords at the sides for a customized fit. There are also straps on the shoulders to accommodate a wider frame, or if you want the vest to sit a little lower on your torso. For reference, I have mine on the shortest setting.

Sources indicate that one downside of the G-Vest is its limited size options. There are only two: S/M or L/XL. I highly recommend using the size chart to determine which fit is best for you. I’m typically a medium when shopping for athletic tops, but I chose the L/XL because my chest circumference is on the cusp of both options. It’s also worth mentioning that the weight of the S/M vest is four pounds and 12 ounces, while the L/XL is five pounds and six ounces.

Read More: Omorpho G-Vest Review.

According to recent reports, you can shell out up to $300 for a weighted vest, but not everyone needs all the extra features that come with that higher price tag. The ApexUp weighted vest is a popular option thanks to its low price point, but it offers more than just savings.

Industry observers note that this vest is built from neoprene (which is the durable synthetic rubber you’ll find in wetsuits) and filled with iron sand, a material that’s denser than natural sand and absorbs less moisture. As a result, it won’t stick to you or clump up when you sweat.

Industry observers note that it has a smooth, comfortable feel, with seams that are stitched over with fabric to prevent rubbing and chafing. Wide armholes and an adjustable strap across the chest mean you can get a comfortable fit, no matter your chest size.

Sources indicate that the solo strap in ApexUp’s 10-pound version means it’s more likely to shift around during dynamic movements like burpees, making this vest a better choice for things like walking. A lot of the weight in the vest is in the front straps, so just be aware of your posture while you use this. But the mesh storage pocket in back is secure and roomy enough for your phone, which is a nice feature if you want to free up your hands.

It has been revealed that A common complaint with this vest is the smell, which may be due to that neoprene cover. If you notice it and it bothers you, just let the vest air out a little before using it. Also, be aware that the ApexUp vest doesn’t allow you to tack on extra weight. But at this low price, you can simply buy a latest one when you’re ready for more resistance and still come out on top, price-wise.

The best weighted vest is one you’ll actually wear, and the Stakt Adjustable Weighted Vest makes that part easy. Instead of looking like tactical gear, its streamlined neoprene construction fits close to the body and feels more like a weighted garment.

One way WH fitness and reviews editor Natascha Grief, NASM-CPT likes to use weighted vests in her own training and with her training clients is to increase proprioception, or awareness of the body’s position in space. Because the Stakt vest distributes weight around the torso instead of loading only the shoulders, it can provide helpful feedback for connecting with the core and postural muscles during movement.

The Stakt weighted vest starts at six pounds and a two-pound zip-on extension brings it up to eight pounds. Grief tested both configurations while walking, doing chores around her apartment, doing pushups, and adding it to a functional training workout. It delivered comfortable, evenly distributed weight that fits and feels more like an additional clothing layer than a traditional weighted vest.

According to recent reports, the aluminum front buckles feel sturdy. The shoulder straps use a hook-and-loop adjustment system, so once Grief found the right adjustment, it was a set-it-and-forget-it situation, and the straps stayed put. “I didn’t have to interrupt any workout to readjust them,” she mentioned.

A porous mesh liner creates a comfortable buffer between the body and the neoprene, which adds some breathability. It also zips out for washing, which is a helpful feature, especially considering that this vest is worn close to the body. The vest also has a mesh pocket for small essentials. Its reflective detailing is minimal though, so you’ll want additional visibility gear when walking in low-light conditions.

Read More: Stakt Weighted Vest Review.

If you’re looking for an adjustable-weight option ideal for specific functional training exercises and rucking, the Hyper Vest Elite from Hyperwear is highly customizable. I tested the 10-pound model, which is weighted with 66 individual 2.25-ounce stainless steel bars, each with its own little pocket.

According to recent reports, if you prefer heavier weights, 15- and 20-pound options are available. Plus, you can purchase a box of individual weights to load up your vest (each pocket can fit two 2.25-ounce weights).

In a recent development, I wore it during multiple 60-minute walks, squats, pull-ups, push-ups, and back extensions. With the full 10 pounds loaded on my body, I found it really difficult to do pull-ups and push-ups. However, when I removed some of the weights from the individual pockets, it made for a more manageable load.

That said, I’m not sure how realistic it is to load up these tiny weights into individual pouches when switching between exercises. I think it’s a great feature, but personally, I’d design my workouts to ensure I didn’t have to adjust the weights more than once.

There are adjustable cords on each side to cinch or loosen for your preferred fit, but you won’t find shoulder strap adjustments like on the Omorpho vests. I also noticed the Hyperwear vest sits nearly five inches lower on my torso than the Omorpho vest. It doesn’t dig into my hips, but I notice it grazes my lower back when walking. It’s not a deal breaker, but I prefer shorter styles. Four size options are available: small, medium, large, and extra large.

In a recent development, as for material, I appreciate the heavy-duty construction of this vest, which is made with Cordura, a synthetic, tear-resistant fabric popular for backpacks and military clothing. It will hold up for years, even if you plan to go hiking or wear it in the elements. I also like the reflective strips at the zipper and across the chest for increased visibility outdoors.

If you’re looking for a weighted vest with resistance that pushes your limits while not disrupting your range of motion, this one by Vivitory checks the box. Despite the non-cropped fit, it still stays in place with only two adjustable straps and distributes weight evenly (11 pounds for the medium size and 18 pounds for the large size).

According to recent reports, WH art director Christine Giordano was pleasantly surprised by how light it felt compared to holding it. “I was nervous it was going to be too heavy for me or cause pain in my lower back, but I was wrong,” indicates Giordano. “It didn’t bounce up and down or move all over—it stayed snug to my body while not being too hot and bulky.”.

She loves wearing it during easy walks when waiting around for her kids’ sporting events or for more intense workouts, such as CrossFit or burpees. “I’m not a huge fan of dumbbell step-ups, so I tried it with the vest for the added weight without leaning forward,” she notes.

In a recent development, as for the material, it’s made with neoprene, a synthetic rubber resistant to sweat that Giordano says she found to be breathable. There are also reflective strips on the vest for visibility during dawn or dusk, and a small pouch at the back for holding essentials.

If you get seriously sweaty during cardio or weightlifting, this 12-pound Reebok weighted vest is an option in hot summer temps. The back has a breathable ventilation panel that allows air to circulate.

According to recent reports, WH contributor Korin Miller has recently added it to her workout gear lineup. “I like to go hard with my workouts, and I get really sweaty as a result—I appreciate the open-air design of this vest so I can cool off,” claims Miller. “That, combined with the airy fabric, means I won’t end up with the vest sticking against my skin during workouts.”.

Aside from its sweat-wicking properties, its two adjustable straps allow for a customized fit during a variety of workouts. For Miller, specifically walking, cycling, rowing, and bodyweight movements, such as planks and squats.

But, it’s important to note this model isn’t ideal for jumping. “Those extra weights can flap around during bigger movements like running and HIIT workouts—basically anything that has you jumping up and down,” says Miller.

Read More: Reebok Weighted Vest Review.

It has been revealed that the Omorpho G-Vest Icon is a quality choice for runners and HIIT workouts, given its snug fit and moderate weight that doesn’t feel like too much. The design is really similar to Omorpho’s OG model, with soft neoprene-style fabric, stainless steel ball bearings embedded into the fabric, and waist and shoulder adjustments for a custom fit.

It has been revealed that the main difference is the adjustable weight and reflective strips throughout for extra visibility during night runs. The adjustable weight system is genius. It involves “G-Packs” of varying weights that snap in and out, allowing you to tack on additional, evenly distributed weight fast. (Just a heads up: A set of three G-Packs that brings the weight up to 12 pounds costs an extra $129.).

Recent findings suggest that we also like that the encased stainless steel weights are not featured through the chest area. If you want to wear the G-Vest Icon with just a sports bra, you won’t have any irritation from high-impact movements.

Sources indicate that for reference, the weights go up the entirety of the front panels on the men’s version. While the vest’s fitted style is ideal for runs, its six-pound weight means it’s better suited for things like short runs and sprints.

In a recent development, one downside is that the neoprene-style fabric made our tester sweat a ton when worn with layers. “My first experience with the vest was under my winter jacket on a 10-degree day during an hour-long walk,” WH contributor Korin Miller notes. “I sweat my butt off despite the cold temperatures, compared to having sweat evaporate from my skin at the gym.”.

Read More: Omorpho G-Vest Icon Review.

It has been revealed that besides being a WH Fitness Awards 2025 winner, the Empower Weighted Vest is the only vest we’ve seen with a cross-style fit. It’s designed specifically to fit women’s curves while offering supreme support for the shoulder blades. The fit is compact with less material at the sides, while the straps are fully adjustable.

Recent findings suggest that while its main highlight is being a custom fit for women, another unique feature is six removable one-pound bags (three in the front and three in the back pockets). In the 10-pound model (weight ranges from eight to 16 pounds), the vest can go as low as four pounds when the weights are removed if you’re seeking only light resistance.

WH health and fitness editor Addison Aloian, NASM-CPT, uses it for taking her workouts to the next level. “It elevates my walks, helps my core activate more, and makes my bodyweight exercises harder,” she says. Her only complaint is that the removable weights can make it feel bulky and interfere with hitting the full range of motion with a handful of exercises. “If I wanted to do crunches, I couldn’t lie on my back without it arching, and I couldn’t do supermans from my stomach because the bags in the front made it so I couldn’t lie flat,” she says. “During other strength exercises like squats, it hit the top of my thigh and prevented me from moving down further.” Perhaps it’s best to use the added pocket weights only during walks.

As for material, it’s neoprene for optimal sweat resistance, like the Vivitory and Prodigen weighted vests.

Not everyone wants or needs the 20-pound resistance TRX’s Hexgrip Weighted Vest can offer. But this vest is adjustable, allowing you to tweak the weight in one-pound increments, giving you room to grow up to that 20 pounds. So, if you want to use it as a 10-pound vest to start, more power to you.

Sources indicate that this sturdy vest helps you get a secure fit with the help of three wide Velcro straps, making it a solid option for dynamic movements, some cardio workouts, and general strength training. The neoprene inner is comfortable against your skin, while the snug fit and smartly positioned weights mean you don’t have to stress about the vest moving around on you while you work out.

According to recent reports, while it’s on the heavier end, it’s not bulky. As a result, you can still feel comfortable doing your usual range of motion. Just a heads up: Some of the weights are positioned across the chest, which may feel more noticeable if you have larger breasts. But those adjustable straps mean you can lower or raise the shoulder straps to find a position that’s more comfortable for you.

According to recent reports, the weights slip into individual pockets to prevent them from shifting around, but make sure they’re secured well before you start your workout. (Some people have reported them sliding out.) Because the adjustment process takes some time, this isn’t a vest you’ll want to adjust mid-workout. This vest also comes in a 40-pound version, although most exercisers will do best with the 20-pounder as a heavy option.

Sources indicate that if you have broader shoulders, the RITFIT has fully adjustable straps. They're spaced further apart—one sits higher on your chest and the other closer to your waist.

In a recent development, it can be more comfortable if you have a larger chest, while it may run bigger on smaller frames. It also has mesh pockets to store your keys and phone.

The load on a weighted vest can range from 3 to over 30 pounds, depending on the style and brand. If you’ve never used a weighted vest or are new to resistance training, I recommend starting with a lighter option between 3 and 10 pounds. Our best overall pick is optimal for newbies since it’s five pounds.

Heavier vests are ideal for loading bodyweight exercises like push-ups, pull-ups, squats, and walking lunges. They can also be used for walking, hiking, or rucking, depending on your fitness level. Lighter vests are ideal for speed training like sprinting, interval training, and plyometric exercises like box jumps, burpees, or jump roping.

Durable materials such as Cordura, nylon, and polyester are less likely to tear from constant wear during intense movement. All of the picks on this list are made from either of these three fabrics, and I found they perform well during explosive workouts and cardio. They also wick away sweat, which is a must for ultimate comfort. As for fit, I love an adjustable closure system with a zipper or buckles at the front, waist, and shoulders for customizing the fit.

Sources indicate that since 2020, we’ve updated this story and tested every major weighted vest on the market. I’m a certified personal trainer with the National Strength and Conditioning Association. I’ve worked in the health and fitness industry for nine years and have six years of hands-on experience working with clients one-on-one and in small group settings. With experience testing and reviewing hundreds of fitness products over the years, I wore select weighted vests for multiple hour-long walks and workouts, including exercises like push-ups, pull-ups, lunges, planks, and box jumps. I paid close attention to the material to see how it held up against sweat, fit for comfort, and weight for resistance levels. I also kept notes of my likes and dislikes.

According to recent reports, WH editors, including associate health and fitness editor Addison Aloian, NASM-CPT, art director Christine Giordano, and contributor Korin Miller, also tested a few options and provided extensive notes on their experiences with them. Read on for our thoughts on the best weighted vests for women, as well as some other recommendations we like but haven't tested personally.

Sources indicate that lauren Strong is a NSCA-Certified Personal Trainer who has worked in the health and fitness industry for almost a decade. She coaches clients on the fundamentals of dumbbell and barbell training in one-on-one and group settings. She has also tested and reviewed over 200 fitness products and supplements for Garage Gym Reviews.

In a recent development, jacqueline Andriakos, CPT, is the executive health and fitness director at Women’s Health, where she oversees all health and fitness content across WomensHealthMag.com and the print magazine. She has more than a decade of experience covering the wellness space and has edited ASME-nominated health features, spearheaded brand packages such as Fitness Awards, and represented the brand on the TODAY show, podcasts, and more. Before Women's Health, Jacqueline was the deputy health features editor at Self.com, and previously worked as the senior editor at Health magazine. As a writer-reporter, she has contributed to print and online publications including TIME, Real Simple, and People, among others. A dancer throughout her youth, Jacqueline went on to study journalism at the Medill School of Journalism at Northwestern University and stoked her passion for health and fitness during her college years, ultimately inspiring her to make women’s health content the focus of her media career. She is constantly researching the latest health and wellness trends, trying a buzzy new workout class, hiking and snowboarding, or browsing athleisure. Her friends would describe her as the confidant to turn to for fitness and wellness advice, not to mention answers to any weird body questions. Jacqueline is also a former group exercise instructor and is a certified personal trainer via the National Academy of Sports Medicine (NASM).

Natascha Grief is the fitness and reviews editor for Women’s Health. She writes about fitness, health, performance, everyday movement, and the products that help people train and recover better. She brings more than a decade of experience as a NASM-certified personal trainer focused on training women, with specialties in functional strength training, corrective exercise, nutrition, and behavior change. New Orleans. Charleston. Nashville. Miami. Some of the nation’s most distinctive cities are found in the Southeast, each one celebrated for its unique architecture, music, cuisine, and mix of cultures. The photographers listed below capture the personality of each vibrant city—not to mention the more rural beauty of the lakefronts, coastline, and countryside in between them. Maximizing natural light and architectural details, these photographers imbue their home photos with Southern hospitality. Read on for AD-approved interior photographers in the Southeast.

A bathroom overlooking the Tred Avon River in Maryland, designed by Weeth Home.

Fascinated by homes since she was a child, Keyanna Bowen, who was raised in Maryland, used to scrawl out floor plans from the open houses she visited with her mother. Today, through her studio East & Lane, she captures interiors with wonderful sensitivity to light, texture, and atmosphere.

A Tennessee bedroom makes the most of lakefront views.

There’s more to Joseph Bradshaw’s portfolio than a well-appointed room. The Nashville photographer maintains an extensive personal practice, including songwriting, alongside design commissions, with Sarah Sherman Samuel, Pursley Dixon, and April Tomlin among the talents he has worked with.

Find your next creative collaborator using the AD PRO Sourcebook. Start exploring top interior photographers, stylists, decorative painters, millworkers, and more now.

A Miami guest suite by Moniomi Design sets a gold standard.

According to recent reports, miami has personality to spare, and Jeanne Michelle Canto has no shortage of subjects to match. Working as JNNS, she has photographed many art-filled homes—including one for AD Spain—and collaborated with Moniomi and Crosby Studios.

The dining nook of an artist’s home in Nashville designed by Pfeffer Torode.

Ask any interior photographers in the Southeast—Southern design takes many forms. Ali Harper’s portfolio offers a place to explore them. The Atlanta photographer has worked with Betsy Brown, Pfeffer Torode, and Paul Bates, alongside assignments spanning hospitality, lifestyle, and product photography.

Interior design by Laura Hodges.

Industry observers note that jennifer Hughes’s interiors and architecture work has been published in a wide range of shelter publications, including AD, Elle Decor, Domino, Dwell, and House Beautiful. The East Coast talent and graduate of Maryland Institute College of Art is sought out for her artful compositions and keen use of light and shadow.

The carriage house of the 1803 Sword Gate House in Charleston.

Come for the Cortney Bishop interiors; stay for the food, travel, and analogue projects. Charleston-based Katie Charlotte Lybrand’s portfolio celebrates architecture and interior decor but leaves room for life beyond the home.

A powder room by Life of Plenty.

It has been revealed that former music producer Justin March brings an ear for nuance to the visual world. He starts by studying a room’s existing light, proportions, and mood, then refines the frame to convey what its designer intended the viewer to feel.

In the historic Upcoming Orleans cottage updated by architect Bryan Young with his client Sukey Novogratz, music and laughter are never in short supply.

All the charm and character of Newly introduced Orleans’s historic architecture shines through in Jacqueline Marque’s photography, which highlights the rich colors, fine details, and storied feel for which the city and its spaces are renowned.

Inside a Northeast cabin retreat.

Industry observers note that if color and lighting are your things, you’ll likely resonate with Anna Naphtali. The editorial section of the Charlotte photographer’s website is organized into four categories: bright, light, soft, and dark. Naphtali’s portfolio also includes music, TV, and fashion work, as well as commercial styling.

Inside a Ryan Millsap-designed residence in Atlanta.

In a recent development, this lensman’s interest in architecture was piqued early on: He was fascinated by buildings and dump trucks as a child. An Atlanta-based talent, Matt Odom covers a range of sectors from architecture to construction, working with industry leaders such as Gensler, Beckhoff, and Robins & Morton.

Sharp, saturated, and rich in detail, Venjhamin Reyes’s bold images of spaces in Florida and beyond have covered several regional magazines and have also been featured across major international media outlets.

Bright and airy interiors are Alyssa Rosenheck’s calling card.

In a recent development, alyssa Rosenheck specializes in light, bright, and white interiors photography. The creative also works as a writer and a public speaker. Her work has been published widely and she is the author of the 2020 book The New Southern Style.

Lauren Sullivan of Well By Design designed her own home in Tennessee.

It has been revealed that for a peek at what’s happening in Nashville beyond the music scene, look to Caroline Sharpnack. The interiors photographer has worked with Vernich Interiors, JFY Designs, and Parkes & Lamb Interiors, with Well by Design also in the mix.

Featuring interiors by Strang Design, a magical Florida home echoes the fabled Hanging Gardens of Babylon.

In a recent development, although Kris Tamburello’s style favors bold and graphic interiors, he’s still able to portray subtlety thanks to his detailed viewpoint and technical proficiency. Based in Miami since 2015, he also frequently travels to New York and throughout the US and Europe for client work.

T Bone Burnett and Callie Khouri own this home in Nashville—but don’t tell their dogs that!

The sun is (almost) always shining in Brie Williams’s work, whether she’s shooting T Bone Burnett and Callie Khouri’s airy home in Nashville or the Goldeneye resort in Jamaica. But she’s just as skilled at playing with the light in moodier interiors such as the Hotel Peter & Paul in New Orleans or artist William Rushton’s loft in Birmingham, Alabama.

James Carville and Mary Matalin’s Virginia home, designed by Cameron Ruppert.

Both a photographer and a fine artist, Stacy Zarin Goldberg’s work has been exhibited in galleries and is regularly featured in local, regional, and national publications.

#64280. The Best Men's Boots, Tested by Style Editors

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Menshealth ↗ Open Full Page

The Best Men's Boots, Tested by Style Editors

📅 17 Feb 2022 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3124 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Menshealth

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that I DIDN’T START out as a “boot guy.” I always thought they were clunky, poorly stitched and didn’t provide enough insole support like my favorite Nike Air Force 1s.
  • Recent findings suggest that since then, the Men’s Health style team and I have tested well over 50 pairs across every silhouette imaginable: cowboy boots, hiking boots, waterproof commuters, dressier Chelsea styles, heritage work boots—the whole lineup.
  • The iconic Blundstone #585 still reigns supreme for its comfort, durability, and style.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that I DIDN’T START out as a “boot guy.” I always thought they were clunky, poorly stitched and didn’t provide enough insole support like my favorite Nike Air Force 1s. But 15 years ago, I bought my first pair of Timberland 6-Inch Premium Boots because a brutal winter hit the East Coast, and slipping around in sneakers wasn’t going to cut it. I needed something that could survive the rain, snow, and slush. It didn’t take long to realize that once fall hits, having a solid pair (or two) in rotation is a non-negotiable. That first leather lace-up carried me through snowball fights and more than a few questionable bar floors—and it sold me on what a good boot can do.

Recent findings suggest that since then, the Men’s Health style team and I have tested well over 50 pairs across every silhouette imaginable: cowboy boots, hiking boots, waterproof commuters, dressier Chelsea styles, heritage work boots—the whole lineup. I’ve worn them on shoots, to weddings, on rainy office days, and on long travel runs, and I can confirm: not every boot is bulky. The right pair can feel as clean and sleek as your favorite sneakers. So if you’re looking for something versatile enough to move from the office to the bar or carry you from one event to the next, we’ve got you covered. Our picks deliver comfort, durability, and style, whether you need a tough trail option, something practical for wet commutes, or a sleek pair for a night out.

The iconic Blundstone #585 still reigns supreme for its comfort, durability, and style. Part Chelsea boot, part work boot, its leather feels soft with a pre-distressed texture, while inside is cushy and snug from the moment you put it on. We didn’t feel any tightness or have to wait a couple of wears for it to mold to our feet. Our editor Tim Kohut wears it at his standing desk for seven hours straight, and his feet never give in or develop blisters. He even took it on a weekend hike and felt comfortable the whole way, hills, dips, and all. The pull tabs also make it easy to slide your foot in and out.

I’ve worn warmer boots in my testing, but they were much bulkier. This pair has a lighter, slimmer build, yet works for general fall and winter gear. The boot’s leather upper dries in minutes, whether I get caught in light showers or trudge through three inches of snow. Yes, the material can scuff if you’re not careful, but a quick wipe with a damp cloth brings it right back. After months of near-daily wear, the elastic panels haven’t stretched out, the sole hasn’t flattened, and the leather has developed a natural patina versus looking beat up. Underfoot, the synthetic polyurethane midsole feels like a thick layer of cushioning, softening every step, especially on Upcoming York’s uneven sidewalks.

In the toe area, my feet have wiggle room instead of feeling cramped. Whether for style or performance, this boot works in a variety of settings. I’ve worn mine with a sweater and dark denim for dinner as well as chinos for the office, and it pairs seamlessly with any casual staples like a flannel overshirt, tee, and jeans under a fall jacket. The price tag may give you pause, but most boots that I’ve spent over $100 on are worth it. You don’t have to baby this one. It looks good as new after being worn everywhere, so it’s a reliable option for work, travel, and trail.

Read More: Blundstone 585 Chelsea Boot Review.

In a recent development, when our senior fitness and commerce editor Brett Williams slipped into the Beckett Simonon Bolton Chelsea, he immediately called out how sharp it looked. This Chelsea boot—a style originating in 19th-century Britain as a close-fitting riding boot with elastic side panels—elevates whatever you’re wearing. The super premium, full-grain calfskin leather has a natural sheen and structure, and the almond-shaped toe box gives it a sleek profile that reads dressy. Inside, the Vachetta leather lining helped keep his foot cool and surprisingly comfortable after hours at his standing desk.

Brett wore it with suits, dress pants, and black denim on shoot days, and it held up across the board. And yes, Chelseas aren’t strictly “formal only” anymore, but the Bolton proves that a dress-leaning Chelsea can still be incredibly versatile. The stitched construction makes it lighter and more flexible than the typical Goodyear-welted options. It’s easily one of the best leather Chelsea boots on the market because it nails every detail: premium calfskin, a breathable lining, a sleek silhouette, and real comfort. Plenty of Chelseas look the part but feel clunky or overly stiff, so the $279 is justifiable.

Read More: Best Chelsea Boots for Men.

According to recent reports, our grooming editor, Sean Zucker, took the Amberjack Chukka for a proper test run, and he came back raving about how wildly comfortable it felt from the jump. The full-grain leather upper and sheepskin lining give it a polished look, but the real magic is underfoot: the heat-activated insole that molds to your feet after a few wears. Plus, the lightweight outsole feels closer to a cushy sneaker than a traditional boot.

Sean wore it on rainy commutes, into the office, and around the city on weekend errands. He didn’t have any sore arches or slips on wet sidewalks. The leather ages nicely over time, and the overall vibe lands squarely in that “smart casual” sweet spot. It works with chinos and slim trousers, and can stretch to dark denim, but it’s not meant to stand in for a dress boot.

If you’ve dismissed cowboy boots as too costumey, Tecovas offers a sleek option that balances rugged style and pairs with a bunch of casual and dressy fits. The round-toe design features a tough, beautiful cowhide leather that wears well whether you’re dressing up or down. The cowhide leather gives the Cartwright a durable feel, while its classic round toe and signature stitching keep the design recognizable.

Recent findings suggest that surprisingly, I didn’t have to break this boot in. From the first wear, it felt comfortable without any pinching or stiffness. To coincide with the theme, I wore it to Beyoncé’s Cowboy Carter concert in Latest Jersey, and I stood the entire three hours. During the first half of the show, it started lightly raining, but the leather dried in seconds. While it’s not as grippy on slippery surfaces as the Merrell and Timberland boots, it’s stable enough for most city sidewalks. Our editors found it to be suitable for the office, the bar, or even a wedding. It’s one of those boots that you can wear year-round. Tecovas offers a few different colors, but we’re especially into the hazelnut, which looks great with dark jeans or dressier pants.

Industry observers note that what really makes this Tecovas pair stand out is how approachable it feels, especially if you’ve never owned a cowboy boot before. The 12-inch shaft—the part of the boot that rises from your ankle to your lower calf—isn’t overly tall or stiff, so it slips easily under straight or relaxed-fit jeans. Also, the 1½-inch heel is low and manageable, so you get a classic cowboy shape without feeling like you’re walking on a block. Fit-wise, it runs true to size and feels secure without squeezing the instep, which is often the biggest concern with Western-style boots. If you want the look without committing to something flashy or trend-driven, this is a smart, low-risk entry point that still feels elevated.

It has been revealed that timberland’s classic work boot has outlasted trendy styles for decades because it’s durable, has a timeless design, and goes with everything. Aptly named the “Butters”, it’s one of the most recognizable boots because of its signature cut and proportions: the high top, thick lug sole, and warm wheat-colored nubuck leather. It’s become a staple across music, streetwear and sports culture. I’ve had it in rotation since I was a teen and still weave it into my casual fits to this day. Yes, it takes one to three wears to break in, but after that you get a snug, customized fit that you can fine-tune with the laces.

The Timberland boot’s cultural relevance hasn’t slowed down, either. A lot of fashion gents like Timothée Chalamet have been spotted wearing Timberland off-duty and even at red carpet events. It also taps into today’s men’s trends, especially the ongoing ’90s-Y2K revival, where baggier denim, boxy jackets, and easy, layered knits are back in rotation.

It has been revealed that this boot has full-grain and nubuck leather uppers that can handle scuffs and are fully waterproof, so rain and slush never ruin the look. It's sturdier and heavier than most fashion boots, because it was originally built for work, but it doesn't feel like you’re lugging around bricks all day. The bulk is part of the style, and why it pairs so well with relaxed denim, cargos, and winter fits. Whether I’m walking on wet sidewalks or cobblestone, the lug sole feels stable underfoot.

If we’re judging purely on trail performance, the Merrell Thermo Chill 2 is the best pick for hiking. The mid-height design gives your ankles the extra support they need on uneven terrain, so you’re not wobbling around. Most hiking boot outsoles rely on standard rubber compounds that work well, but they usually sacrifice grip for durability or flexibility. With 200g insulation, this style makes for a perfect winter boot.

It’s fully waterproof, so puddles, rain, or soggy grass aren’t going to slow you down. The main draw here is the exclusive footbed, which molds to your foot, over time, giving each step a cushioned, natural feel. Brower wore this boot on a weekend camping trip, splashing through soggy trails and wet grass, and by the end of it, his feet were dry and comfortable. The mesh on the tongue keeps things breathable, too, so when the sun comes out, your feet don’t feel like they’re baking. While it’s not as sleek as the Danner boot, it’s still a solid-looking boot that you can wear off the trail.

Most rugged boots are kind of ugly, but Danner delivers a trail-ready option that actually looks sharp. The rich tan color paired with red laces gives it a bold yet unique look for the trail. Outside of hikes, our Tech and Gear editor Ryan Brower likes to style it with a flannel shirt and jeans. He’s been wearing it consistently over the last couple fall seasons. It’s not the warmest option in freezing 30-degree temps, so it might be wise to wear with thicker socks. It’s made with full-grain leather uppers, which age beautifully and bead off rain. Plus, the waterproof liners keep water from getting inside.

Full-grain leather is also tougher and more durable than corrected grain or split leather (found in cheaper boots) that have been sanded or split down, losing their outer layers. The break-in period takes a little patience, but after a few wears, this boot feels comfortable and natural. The Vibram outsole grips especially well on uneven terrain, whether you’re climbing trails in the Oregon mountains or navigating slick city streets in New York. Between the outsole and insole, there’s a fiberglass shank—a thin, supportive layer that reinforces the midfoot. It helps keep your feet stable, prevents the boot from twisting, and reduces fatigue on long walks.

In a recent development, red Wing has been crafting durable, American-made workwear for more than a century, supplying tradesmen, factory workers and miners with boots built to last. The Classic Moc Boot continues that tradition with a roomy moc toe, weatherproof leather construction, and a comfortable wedge sole that makes long hours on your feet far more manageable. (A moc toe is a stitched toe design where the seam wraps around the front of the boot, giving extra room and durability.).

It has been revealed that men’s Health designer Jason Speakman broke it in on a hike in upstate Latest York. Since the leather is a bit hefty, it did take some getting used to. But after about two or three wears, he mentioned it didn’t feel as cramped as other moc toe boots he's tested. There was no strain on his feet after going from rocks to packed trails, and they stayed comfortable even on uneven terrain. Aesthetically, it has the rugged, All-American vibe that works on a job site, weekend trail, or just rolling up to the beer hall in jeans. The full-grain oiled leather is super premium, so this option will last years and develop a cool, worn-in patina.

Industry observers note that after doing some work in the yard for hours on end, Speakman found the EVA midsole—which is a foam material that’s both lightweight and strong—makes this boot the most comfortable option for raking leaves and pushing a lawnmower. It also handles hard surfaces like concrete or brick, keeping your feet cushioned and protected from constant pounding.

If you’re looking for a hiking boot that won’t make your wallet flinch but still performs like something far more expensive, the Nortiv8’s offering is an easy win. On the trail it proved, while affordable, that it’s not cheaply made. Right out of the box, the waterproof synthetic leather and textile upper felt surprisingly substantial—not floppy or flimsy like some lower-cost boots. The material stood up to brush and rocks on a muddy forest loop, and after hours of hauling gear and setting up camp in wet grass, it still looked crisp with no signs of fraying.

The waterproof membrane lived up to its promise during shallow creek crossings and soggy morning hikes; my socks stayed dry every time, even when water pooled around my feet. Underfoot, the rubber lug outsole delivered dependable traction. I tested it while fishing and the grip felt stable and sturdy. The midsole’s cushioned EVA foam struck a nice balance too: supportive on long miles but soft enough that my feet didn’t feel trashed by day’s end. It’s not an ultralight trail runner, but for hiking, camping, fishing, and general outdoor wear, the way these materials work together is impressive for the price.

Not many boots can pull off a tailored suit, but Frye’s luxe ankle style is the rare exception. I’ve been wearing mine for the past couple months, and it instantly makes any semi-formal fit feel sharper. The design is simple but polished with a premium leather upper and is stitched around the edge for extra durability. I wore it in light rain and the material dried in seconds. I also found the inner-side zipper makes life so much easier when I’m slipping it on and off after a long day. It was refreshing that it didn’t require an annoying break-in period. When I first tried it on, I realized I had wiggle room in the toe area right away.

After five wears, the leather starts to crease naturally, but that adds personality to the boot without it looking worn. I’ve tested it on city streets and light rain, and the grip is solid enough to feel confident walking anywhere without slipping or scuffing the leather. The ankle height is flattering, the shape is not heavy-looking, and the richness of the leather colors pairs with different outfits. You can rock jeans and a sweater for a casual lunch, or dress it up with slacks and a blazer.

According to recent reports, sure, this boot isn’t cheap, but the quality, durability, and timeless design make it worth the investment. You’re paying for a boot that will remain in good condition for years, look better as it ages, and feel comfortable from day one.

Recent findings suggest that leather is a reliable choice for everyday boots because it can be durable and develop character with wear. Full-grain and nubuck each have their own look and feel, but neither guarantees waterproof protection on its own. If you’re regularly walking through rain or slush, look for a waterproof membrane or specifically waterproof construction.

Recent findings suggest that EVA foam midsoles are lightweight and cushioned, perfect for long days on your feet. Some boots use polyurethane midsoles, which are a bit heavier but offer more durability and stability, especially if you’re on rugged terrain.

Sources indicate that your traction and durability depend on this part. Vibram outsoles are often considered the gold standard for their grip and long-lasting wear. Rubber outsoles are common on everyday and outdoor boots because they can provide traction and abrasion resistance. Grip varies by rubber compound and tread pattern, so look for an outsole designed for the surfaces and conditions you’ll encounter.

Industry observers note that goodyear-welted boots can be a good investment because their construction often allows the outsole to be replaced when it wears down. The welt can also help limit water intrusion, although the construction alone doesn’t make a boot waterproof.

Our fashion team, led by longtime boots enthusiast and Style and Reviews Director Christian Gollayan, found the most comfortable and durable options out there. We put more than 50 pairs of boots through the wringer, wearing them across cobblestone New York streets, rainy city commutes, long-distance hikes, and casual weekends around town. In each test, we looked closely at grip, how the soles handled slick surfaces, insulation to keep feet warm in cold weather, and waterproofing to make sure soggy socks weren’t part of the deal. We also rewarded boots that could pull double duty: looking sharp with dress pants or a suit while still holding up for more rugged, off-duty wear.

BYD and Geely approached FIA about a 12th F1 team, says Ben Sulayem

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1026 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • BYD and Geely have both approached the FIA about entering Formula 1, the sport’s governing body confirmed.
  • Recent findings suggest that but there’s no open process for a 12th team, and neither firm has a deal.
  • “One of them was BYD and another was Geely,” Ben Sulayem said of the manufacturers that have reached out about joining the grid.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

BYD and Geely have both approached the FIA about entering Formula 1, the sport’s governing body confirmed. FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem named the two Chinese automakers while speaking at the Newly introduced Economy Forum in Madrid, as first reported by Grande Prêmio.

Recent findings suggest that but there’s no open process for a 12th team, and neither firm has a deal. The FIA is also pushing F1 toward the kind of engine an EV maker has the least reason to build.

“One of them was BYD and another was Geely,” Ben Sulayem said of the manufacturers that have reached out about joining the grid.

He remarked he suggested that BYD buy an existing team instead of starting a fresh one. BYD wasn’t interested in that route. It wants its own team, so Ben Sulayem told the firm to come back with a “serious proposal” that demonstrates the project can work.

According to recent reports, he also made it clear that Chinese manufacturers won’t get special treatment. Any bid would go through the same process as other prospective entrants, and the rules won’t be rewritten to suit them. Right now, there’s no expansion process at all: the FIA isn’t actively looking for a 12th team.

Still, Ben Sulayem repeated that he’d like F1’s next newcomer to come from China, pointing to the country’s EV technology and the Chinese Grand Prix in Shanghai.

This isn’t upcoming for BYD. Back in March, we reported that BYD was exploring a Formula 1 entry, either by buying a team or building one from scratch.

According to recent reports, in April, executive vice president Stella Li said BYD had met F1 CEO Stefano Domenicali in Shanghai and that an entry was “something we’re discussing.” By July, the tone had cooled. Li said “the dream is always there, but we don’t have a concrete agenda,” and special advisor Alfredo Altavilla set a clear condition: “We will never participate in Formula 1 just to put a sticker on the side of a car.”.

Altavilla said BYD would only consider F1 to the extent its technology can serve the sport.

Industry observers note that geely is the new name here. The group sold 3.02 million vehicles last year and owns Volvo, Polestar, and Lotus, a brand with decades of F1 history. It’s also heading into Canada next year as Chinese automakers push hard into new markets.

The last newcomer, Cadillac, took a long road. The FIA opened an expression-of-interest process in 2023, and GM’s team only joined the grid as the 11th team this season, running Ferrari power until its own power unit arrives. Audi got in the other way, by taking over Sauber.

Here’s where it gets awkward for an EV maker. The 2026 F1 power units split output roughly 50/50 between the combustion engine and electric power, with the MGU-K jumping to 350 kW.

The FIA is already walking that back. In June, it agreed to shift the split to 60-40 in favor of combustion for 2027 and 2028. And Ben Sulayem has been pushing for V8 engines running on sustainable fuel with “minor electrification” for the next rules cycle, starting in 2031 at the latest, possibly 2030. Domenicali says F1 should have a package ready to discuss by the end of this year.

So the FIA president wants a Chinese EV maker on the grid, while pushing a rulebook that makes their main strength less relevant.

We like the idea of BYD or Geely in F1. Chinese automakers have the money and the engineers, and they badly need brand prestige outside China. BYD in particular has been on a performance push with Yangwang, and F1 would be the loudest possible way to tell Europe it’s not just a cheap car brand.

It has been revealed that they look for visibility/recognition on the world stage, regardless EVs. And in some (primitive) markets they market themselves as hybrids automakers, not as EV automakers.

They will make a hybrid power unit (which they already make anyway) to comply with the backward F1 regulations.

But Ben Sulayem’s comments don’t move things much. There’s no entry process, BYD has already turned down his main suggestion, and Geely’s interest is a name dropped at a conference, not a bid.

A Chinese would likely be good for F1 as well. Motorsports are on the rise in China, and that would be the cherry on top in helping popularize the sport in the world’s largest market.

Recent findings suggest that the bigger issue is the engine. Altavilla was clear that BYD isn’t interested in slapping a logo on a car. It wants F1 to showcase its technology, and BYD’s technology is batteries and electric drive. The FIA’s V8 push goes the other way. It’s hard to sell an EV giant on a sport that’s reducing the electric part of the powertrain.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

After years of chunky dad sneakers and super-technical running shoes taking over the fashion scene, we're seeing a return to slimmer sneaks. And few shoes have made a bigger impression on that front than the Puma Speedcat OG. First launched in 1999, its streamlined fit and lower platform take cues from Formula 1 footwear. Now it’s found a second life as a street-style favorite. I see it constantly on the streets of NYC, and it’s become just as much of a fixture during my travels to fashion capitals like London and Paris. So I finally got my hands on the cute, comfortable sneaker, and after more than two months of testing, I understand the obsession.

According to recent reports, the slender sneaker sits very low to the ground, giving it that ballet-flat silhouette which makes it feel much more like a fashion shoe than an athletic sneaker. Ballet-inspired shoes and “sneakerinas” are increasingly popular these days, styled with streetwear fits by celebs like Dua Lipa and Emily Ratajkowski. The buttery suede upper and lithe shape give similar kicks—like the Adidas Samba—a run for their money with a more luxe feel, separating the Speedcat from court sneakers and tennis shoes. I wear mine constantly with a simple straight-leg jean and sweater outfit formula or mix things up with something like a linen pant and leather jacket. I love how the Speedcat adds an edgy, cool-girl feel to my outfits without much styling effort. It’s also a nice change of pace from the chunkier running shoes I typically gravitate toward.

The pliable upper and sturdy heel collar make it easy to slip on and go when I’m in a rush. And darting around to catch a train is also not a problem for the Speedcat: There's very little bulk between your foot and the ground, so the shoe moves naturally with you rather than feeling like you're lugging around a chunky sneaker. One unexpected perk? I'm obviously not navigating an F1 track anytime soon, but I love driving in this shoe. I spend a lot of time behind the wheel on Long Island, and the Speedcat is one of my favorite shoes to wear for endless errands and longer drives. The thin sole doesn't get in the way of the pedals, and I can actually feel what I'm doing with my feet.

That said, this doesn’t provide the same level of comfort and cushioning you’d find in one of our favorite walking shoes, the Hoka Clifton 11. There's minimal shock absorption underfoot, so I wouldn't choose it for a day involving miles of walking or when I’ll be on my feet from morning ‘til night. I find it comfortable for my everyday routine, particularly when I'm driving, running errands, commuting to work, or heading out for a casual day. The fit is also on the snug side, especially through the toe box. If you have wider feet or prefer a roomier sneaker, I'd keep that in mind before buying and probably size up.

In a recent development, one thing I have been impressed with is how well the Speedcat OG has held up. Most suede uppers are tough to clean, but this one still looks great after more than two months of regular wear (including getting caught in the rain), and the outsole has a grippy feel even on wet sidewalks. Despite its lighter weight, my feet feel locked in during everyday activities. It’s not a sneaker I'd choose for a workout or any activity that requires a lot of lateral movement and support, but that's not really what it's designed for.

The Puma Speedcat OG has earned a permanent spot in my shoe rotation, and I’m already thinking about which colorways I’ll be adding to my collection next. It's not the most cushioned sneaker I own, but as someone who loves a good fashion sneaker, it’s become my capsule wardrobe holy grail. So if you're willing to trade a little underfoot cushioning for a seriously good-looking, lightweight sneaker, I think the Speedcat OG lives up to the hype.

#64273. The 6 Best Brooks Shoes for Walking, Tested By Style and Fitness Editors

📅 28 Jun 2024 • ⏱️ 14m • 📚 Deep Dive (2888 w)

The 6 Best Brooks Shoes for Walking, Tested By Style and Fitness Editors

📅 28 Jun 2024 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2888 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Womenshealthmag

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in.
  • I’ve been known to have questionable standards in some areas of life—like my preference for boxed wine post-grad or my ability to convince myself that cereal counts as dinner.
  • Brooks has been around for over 100 years, and the brand has perfected its walking (and running) shoes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

I’ve been known to have questionable standards in some areas of life—like my preference for boxed wine post-grad or my ability to convince myself that cereal counts as dinner. But when it comes to what I put on my feet, the bar is high. I used to think a good walking shoe just meant something that didn’t give me blisters. Now, as a style writer with a pile of sneakers so high it rivals Everest, I expect a lot more. I’m talking support, tons of comfort, and yes, style. That’s exactly why Brooks has become my go-to. The brand’s secret sauce: a perfectly balanced, firm-yet-plush cushioning that makes long days on my feet feel like a walk in the park.

Brooks has been around for over 100 years, and the brand has perfected its walking (and running) shoes. It’s no wonder that Brooks sneakers also come highly recommended by our team of active editors and podiatrist Brad Schaeffer, DPM. “Brooks has always been one of my go-to shoes, especially for walking,” claims Schaeffer. That’s thanks to their ideal balance of comfort and support, extensive sizing, secure laces, and breathable, sturdy mesh uppers. You need a shoe specifically for walking because it offers the necessary cushion to take the impact off your joints and give your foot the support it needs to propel forward. These features help prevent aches and injuries.

Industry observers note that there’s a seemingly endless amount of sneakers to choose from, but don’t stress: I’ve put in the work to try out the best Brooks shoes for walking. I log (at least) 10,000 steps per day between walking my energetic Jack Russell terrier all around Long Island and commuting into Manhattan for work. Our team of editors also tested every Brooks sneaker through power walking, long days at the office, and leisurely strolls. Our favorite shoe of the bunch is the Brooks Adrenaline GTS 25, but many others came close for their cushion and stability.

After testing dozens of shoes, the Brooks Adrenaline GTS 26 takes the crown as my go-to for walking (and tbh, everything else). The latest Adrenaline GTS iteration still nails the balance between cushion and support, keeping my stride steady without feeling stiff or squished—which is exactly what I loved about the 25.

What really seals the deal? The firm-yet-cozy midsole hugs the foot just right, offering a secure, locked-in feel that still stays comfortable mile after mile. The 26 has about the same amount of cushioning as the previous version (maybeee a tinge more). It’s the perfect amount of cushion to keep feet comfy without sacrificing stability. The mesh upper got an upgrade too, with even more perforations to keep things cool even on the hottest days. I also love that Brooks kept the 10mm heel-to-toe drop (as opposed to the GTS 24's 12mm drop), which helps reduce the potential for strain in the hips and knees. I just snagged the 26 two weeks ago, but so far, I’ve racked up 15+ walking miles and 5 running miles, pain-free.

Recent findings suggest that the previous Adrenaline iteration actually took home the top spot for walking shoes in our 2026 Fitness Awards for its near-perfect balance between cushioning and stability. And so far, the Adrenaline GTS 26 is looking like a superb contender, keeping all of our favorite details of its younger sibling while improving breathability.

My favorite thing about both versions is the shoe’s GuideRails tech, which uses firm foam on either side of the heel to keep feet locked in. The foam is infused with nitrogen, making it super comfortable and lightweight without being overly plush. Bonus: The (did I mention breathable?) mesh upper keeps things comfy without too much stretch (key for stability while walking), Schaeffer states.

Sources indicate that one heads-up: the Adrenaline GTS 26 is one of the heavier shoes on this list at 9.6 oz., so if you like a super lightweight shoe, you may want to consider the Glycerin Flex. However, I actually find this sneaker feels way lighter thanks to the mesh upper.

Read More: Brooks Adrenaline GTS 25 Review.

Recent findings suggest that if versatility is your priority, the Brooks Ghost 18 delivers. With its nitrogen-fused cushioning, the latest version of the shoe packs in the same amount of plush padding that we loved in the Ghost 17 (it was a 2025 WH Sneaker Award winner for a reason!). Impressively, the moderately high stack height at the heel doesn’t feel too squishy or wobbly. It’s a great do-it-all shoe for long walks, standing all day, and running.

Industry observers note that upgrades from the previous version include a latest sockliner that makes for a comfy, snug fit and a flat tongue (the old one was a more classic padded option). “It does a good job of hugging the shape of your ankle without rubbing or chafing,” says fitness writer and WH contributor Korin Miller. “I like the smooth, seamless feel it creates, but I noticed that the edges start to curl in with repeated use.” I’ve noticed the same, but it’s definitely not an glitch once your foot is in the shoe—just something to double-check when you slide your foot in.

In a recent development, I’ve worn these for long walks with my pup, all-day errands, a Costco shopping spree (IYKYK), and a full day on my feet at a music festival—and my arches stayed happy through it all. The soft midsole offers that just-right level of give that absorbs impact without feeling too soft or marshmallowy. The knit mesh upper is even more breathable than in the last version, adding to the barely-there feel, as does the plush ankle collar, which doesn’t chafe or rub at all.

Industry observers note that one of my only gripes about the Ghost 17 was the slightly narrow toe box, but thankfully, the Ghost 18 solved this problem for me. It’s much more spacious now, both in terms of width and height.

Read More: Brooks Ghost 18 Review.

It has been revealed that if you’re after a walking shoe that’s super cushy, the Brooks Glycerin 23 is it. I’ve tested these on nearly 10-mile walks through nature preserves and standing for hours at the DMV (ugh). I never once felt like my feet were sore or that I needed to rush to sit down—these things felt like walking on pillows.

In a recent development, but the cushioning isn’t the only win here. The Glycerin 23’s knit upper gives this shoe a sock-like feel that hugs your foot without squeezing. It’s smooth, stretchy, and breathable, making it one of the most comfortable shoes I’ve worn on long walks. The shoe has a mild heel drop that helps distribute pressure evenly across the foot and reduces foot fatigue, which I sometimes experience with other walking shoes. While I wouldn’t quite describe the shoe as sleek or minimalist, it balances its plush cushioning with a more understated silhouette (aka it doesn’t veer into chunky dad shoe territory).

It has been revealed that I also appreciate how well this shoe performs on uneven surfaces thanks to its wide platform and ample traction. The durable outsole covers plenty of ground, and the traction has a complex, winding tread pattern. I never feel like I’m going to slip, even on slick pavement.

In a recent development, so far, the Glycerin 23 does a great job of keeping my feet locked in despite its super thick cushioning—but it’s not designed for max stability. Those with specific foot problems, like plantar fasciitis or complications with overpronation, may want to pick a slightly less cushioned, more supportive shoe, like the Adrenaline GTS 25.

Read More: The Best Shoes For Standing All Day.

The Brooks Ghost Max 3 took home the top spot in our guide to the most comfortable sneakers for its perfect balance of maximum support and cushioning. It keeps my feet comfortably locked in, even after hours of wear, and my ankles never feel wobbly, which often happens with plush shoes like this one.

Recent findings suggest that “Out of all the sneakers I’ve tried, I find myself wearing the Brooks Ghost Max 3—it’s the newest addition to the Ghost Max series—the most when I want to feel comfortable during walks or runs (yep, it can do both!),” says style contributor Lily Wohlner. I agree. That’s because the rocker bottom sole, which has a slight curve to it like a rocking chair, helps propel my foot forward with less energy. Wearing it almost feels like walking on a moving runway at the airport.

Even for a max cushioned shoe, it’s super stable thanks to its signature Guardrails tech (the same found in the Adrenaline GTS 25). The outsole also has a broad base, which reduces rolling of the foot inward and outward and cradles the foot in place without interfering with your stride. Fitness contributor Talene Appleton says these features are great for high arches. After hours of walking, she doesn’t feel one ounce of pain or discomfort. And if you have wide feet or bunions, you’re in luck—this shoe comes in both wide and extra-wide options.

During testing, we did notice some wear and tear on the upper pretty early on (after a few months). While it was a bit of a bummer, the elite combo of cushion and support keeps this kick high on my list of Brooks sneakers.

Read more: Best Walking Shoes for Women.

It has been revealed that think of the Glyceric Flex as Glycerin 23’s lighter, more flexible counterpart. The upper and outsole are both made from super bendy materials that give the shoe an almost barefoot feel.

Sources indicate that I’m a substantial fan of this shoe for walking, long periods of standing, running, and plyometric workouts. It's incredibly versatile, thanks to ample nitrogen-infused cushioning and a flexible midsole. The FlexZone technology—a strategically placed groove in the center of the shoe’s outsole—helps enhance the shoe’s flexibility and allows the foot to move naturally. Combined with the pods under the front of the foot (which reminds me of On’s signature CloudTec system you see on most of the brand’s outsoles), the shoe has a super bouncy feel without feeling wobbly.

Bonus: at only 8.0 ounces, it's the lightest shoe on this list, so your feet won’t feel bogged down. But it still falls in Schaeffer’s recommended weight range (eight to 10 ounces), so it's hefty enough to keep your foot locked in. Plus, the flat knit upper is super soft, breathable, and—yes—flexible, which adds to its airy feel.

But the shoe’s lighter weight means it offers less heft and a less supportive feel. If you need more structure or have specific stability needs, these might not be your best bet. But, if you’re into a flexible, responsive shoe that doesn’t weigh you down—this one’s tough to beat.

In a recent development, the Brooks Ghost Max L offers a super plush, easygoing stride. The high-stacked cushioning is next-level—soft but stable, like walking on a marshmallow. It has an outsole with a curved bottom, like a rocking chair, to help propel you forward so each step takes a bit less energy.

It has been revealed that I didn’t expect to notice the rocker bottom that much, but I totally get the hype. Schaeffer indicates he actually prefers rocker-bottom shoes for walking, especially as we get older, because they help take pressure off joints. That mentioned, the same rocker technology makes me feel a little off-balance when I try to run or power walk in them, so I keep these strictly for leisurely walks and casual wear.

Industry observers note that looks-wise, I’m team Ghost Max L all the way. Some might say the stacked foam gives grandma shoes, but I think it strikes that perfect balance of chunky and cool—especially when styled right. I like to wear mine with a wide-leg pant and a blazer on top. It’s got just the right amount of bulk to feel trendy without being clunky, and pairs well with everything from athleisure to workwear.

However, this shoe runs small. Definitely size up if you’re in between sizes or like a little wiggle room. I could have used a half size larger than what I wear in the rest of my Brooks shoes for a little more comfort, but I still get a lot of casual wear out of them regardless.

Industry observers note that first things first, you want a good mix of comfort and stability in your walking shoe, says Schaeffer. He recommends looking for a pair that cups your heel in a way that isn’t too snug or too loose. This feature will keep your feet from wobbling with every step you take. That sort of stability keeps your foot aligned as you walk, which is key for overpronation (foot rolls in too much) or underpronation (foot rolls out), helping prevent strain on your joints and maintaining balance. You want a shoe that’s comfortable on your feet, but Shaeffer says to avoid any that are overly cushioned, and instead look for a shoe that is a bit sturdier to keep your feet in neutral alignment to avoid foot fatigue and prevent sprains or strains.

The front of your sneaker (aka toe box) should never be too snug because it can pinch the nerves and inflame the ball of your foot (aka metatarsalgia). One way to know if your toe box is wide enough? Make sure your foot lies one thumb width from the side of the shoe and one thumb width from the front of the shoe. Tip: If you have a longer second toe, a larger toe box is even more important, Schaeffer claims.

Brooks is famous for its incredible arch support, which is exactly what Schaeffer indicates to look for in a walking shoe. However, if your arches need a little extra TLC, Schaeffer suggests getting insoles that cater to your specific foot needs. He recommends Dr. Scholl’s Multipurpose Insoles or custom orthotics. "The insoles help with alignment and keep you balanced," he says, which is especially notable if you suffer from chronic pain, plantar fasciitis, or issues with your feet rolling inward or outward while you walk. If this sounds like you, we def recommend scheduling a visit with a podiatrist to make sure your feet get the care they need.

Industry observers note that A heel-to-toe drop, sometimes called a midsole drop, is the difference in height between the heel and forefoot (toe area). Schaeffer indicates to look for a walking shoe with a heel-to-toe drop that puts your foot in a neutral position, which will be different for everyone’s unique foot and step pattern.

Schaeffer claims most people love a lightweight shoe since it's nice to feel like there's nothing down there. Just make sure the shoe has a supportive feel, and it holds your foot with every step you take. "In this case, I'm okay with the shoe being light," he says. "But, if the shoe is too light (under four ounces), you sacrifice function and stability." All of the Brooks sneakers on this list are between eight and 10 ounces, so they're the perfect weight in Schaeffer's book.

Sources indicate that over the past two years, the Women’s Health team has undertaken a comprehensive approach to curating the ultimate guide to the best Brooks walking shoes by testing nearly every newly introduced pair as it drops. Along with insights from Brad Schaeffer, DPM, board-certified foot surgeon and owner of Central Park Sole in New York City, we’ve put more than 30 Brooks sneakers through their paces.

According to recent reports, as the associate style and reviews editor, I led the testing process with support from fitness contributor Nicolette Accardi, NASM-CPT, associate health and fitness editor Addison Aloian, NASM-CPT, and fitness and reviews editor Charles Thorp, NASM. Our evaluation involved multiple phases, consulting runners and walkers on the Women's Health team, and most importantly, testing the shoes firsthand. We subjected each shoe to everything from fast walks to long travel days to leisurely strolls. The narrowed-down list above includes the six shoes we were most impressed by.

Previously, she was an assistant editor at Prevention. Shannen graduated from the State University of New York at Cortland with a bachelor's degree in English. If she’s not reading or writing, you can probably find her frequenting the skincare and makeup forums on Reddit or hogging the squat rack at the gym.

Kashmir’s Textile Legacy Inspires a Sumptuous New Line of Home and Fashion Accessories

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (377 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Architecturaldigest

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that few artisanal traditions are so linked with a place that its geographical namesake winds up in the global lexicon.
  • A bouquet of lotus pods held up against the brand’s Mountain blanket in pine.
  • Sources indicate that “It’s the original work-from-home idea,” he says of the technique, passed down for centuries.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that few artisanal traditions are so linked with a place that its geographical namesake winds up in the global lexicon. In the case of fine wool shawls from Kashmir—prized among 19th-century Europeans, including Joséphine Bonaparte—the word cashmere stuck. For Kadri Mujtaba, a fascination with these textiles came early. Born into a family of merchants and weavers in the region’s city of Srinagar, he observed a deep-rooted culture around hand-spun yarn and small wooden looms.

A bouquet of lotus pods held up against the brand’s Mountain blanket in pine.

One of the studio’s handmade shawl looms.

A Doorway Sozni twill blanket draped over a chair.

Sources indicate that “It’s the original work-from-home idea,” he says of the technique, passed down for centuries. Amid encroaching mechanization, Mujtaba has stayed committed to slow craft, cultivating a network of some 2,000 artisans over the past two decades. Initially he’d create custom pieces for designers and brands (Pierre Yovanovitch, The Row, Luis Laplace) and host high-end trunk highlights. That is how Jonathan Renker—via his father, a longtime customer—first encountered the wares. Now, he and Mujtaba have partnered on Kadri: a latest brand of cashmere accessories and home goods that marry Kashmiri refinement and streamlined design.

A Jaali Kaani blanket on the grounds of Pari Mahal garden.

A wood swift of cashmere yarn at the Kadri atelier.

Shawls and scarves from Kadri’s debut collection.

The company debuts with a collection of scarves, throws, and blankets. The cofounders enlisted creative director Dan Thawley and textile designer Maeva Elfassi, who distilled the Kashmir Valley landscape into shades of tobacco, lime, vermilion, and—as a nod to Srinagar’s Dal Lake—dusty blue. Wool from Changthangi goats, which graze across the plateaus of nearby Ladakh, is spun by hand, resulting in airy, ultrasoft knits. More impressive still is the subtlety on display. A bouclé piece has the immersive pull of a Color Field painting, while a quilted scarf joins two paper-thin layers. Just one blanket requires months of work and a balletic dance of bobbins.

“What makes Kadri so special is this research-and-development approach,” says Renker, describing a push toward novel applications while holding fast to the handmade vernacular. “The only electricity that’s used are the overhead lights on a cloudy day.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that BYD’s Flash Charging tech can charge an EV in as little as five minutes. Now, BYD is taking things a step further with integrated solar power and a robotic arm that plugs itself in. See how it all works in action.

After unveiling the Yangwang Altior in the UAE on Monday, its new ultra-luxury flagship electric sedan, BYD showcased its latest breakthrough technology.

The Chinese automaker rolled out a fresh integrated charging system in the Abu Dhabi desert that brings BYD’s “Three Green Dreams” to life.

In 2006, BYD president and CEO Wang Chuanfu revealed his vision of “Three Green Dreams,” including harnessing solar power to generate renewable energy, storing that energy in batteries, and replacing gas-powered vehicles with electric ones that run on clean energy.

The latest charging system is the “world’s first,” according to BYD, to integrate solar power generation, energy storage, Flash Charging, and robotic charging together in one solution.

BYD’s Flash Charging tech enables a vehicle’s battery to charge from 10% to 70% in five minutes, essentially the same time it takes to fill up at a gas station. For a full recharge, or to go from 10% to 97%, it takes just nine minutes.

The fresh robotic charging arm automatically locates the vehicle’s charging port, opens its cover, plugs in, and then removes it once the session is over.

By combining robotic charging with its Automated Valet Parking, BYD stated the latest tech goes beyond automated driving and parking to the charging process itself.

Once the vehicle is parked, the robotic charging arm automatically takes over and connects it to Flash Charging without the driver even touching the cable.

A post shared by Michael Martinez (@mmichael_martinez).

Michaël Martinez, head of marketing at BYD France, posted a video (shown above) showcasing the fresh charging tech in action.

The integrated solution is built around BYD’s Solar-Storage-Charging (SSC) system, fusing solar energy generation, battery storage, and its 5-minute Flash Charging tech. Together, the setup captures energy from the sun, stores it, and distributes it as needed.

If they could tie this into a smart summon type of capability, where the vehicle communicates with the charger and moves the vehicle into the proper location for charging and then moves to a parking spot once charging is complete. Rental car fleets would benefit and so would those in shopping centers. There are so many possibilities and this looks far more mature that the old snake charging Tesla demoed.

BYD has over 16 years of experience in the solar industry with a portfolio that includes solar cells, modules, and systems.

Industry observers note that its solar division, BYD Solar, does business in over 100 countries and regions. By using solar power, BYD stated, the SCC system can operate independently off-the-grid.

Sources indicate that the new technology is part of BYD’s wider Flash Charging rollout. By the end of 2027, the company looks to deploy 6,000 Flash Charging stations globally.
